ROME-TROUGUTS, FROM ABROAD. Oh to be in England Now that April 's there, And whoever wakes in England :lees. some morning, unaware, That the lowest boughs and the brush-wood sheaf Round the elm-tree Dole are in tiny leaf. While the chaffinch sings on the orchard bough In England—flow! And after April, when Mair follows, And the whitethroat builds, and all the swallows! Hark, where my blossomed pear-tree in the hedge Leans to the field and scatters on the clover Blossoms and dewdrops—at the bent sprays hedge— That 's the wise thrush; he sings each song twice over, Lest you should think he never could recapture The first fine careless rapture! And though the fields look rough with hoary dew, All will be gar when noontide wakes anew .The buttercups, the little.children's dower —Far brighter than this gaudy melon-flower! ROBERT BROWNING.

--- - - Good at a pinch—The crab. Running expenses--Children. Modesty is a guard to virtue. To avoid getting wet—Don't go out. A well-wisher—The traveller on the:desert. To keep moths out of your furs—Don't have any. The quail hunter's sport begins-when the game is up. "Pa, what's the dead of night?" "Ghosts, I reckon." Life is not so short but there is always time enough for courtesy. The receiver is as bad as th" thief; but neither of them feels as bad as the loser. However hard up individuals may be, the world has always enough to go round. The difference between a stiff collar and a stiff caller is that one is worn and the other is wearing. "Who is that fellow v.ho has been talking about Withers all the evening!" "That's Withers?' The ear and the eye are the mind's receivers; but the tongue is only busied in expending the treasure received. s.—"Do you know what the dollar sign is, Teddy?" Yeth, urn. It's an eth wiv a wailwoad wunnin' over
it." A.: "When I drink much, I can't work, and so I let it alone." B.: "The drinking?" A.: "No—the
_ working." A PROPER APOLOGY.—" That isn't a very good picture of the baby, is it, Lottie ?" "No, sir; but he isn't a very _
lipid baby:" If a man could be conscious of all that is said of him in his absence he would probably become a:very modest
man indeed. It was a well-meaning citizen who alleged as a reason for not wishing to live on a hill that the climb-it did _ .
_ not suit him. Why do the recriminations of married couples resemble the sound of waves on the shore? Because they are _ . .

murmurs of the tied. What a strange thing matrimony is! Many a hit is made with a miss, and many a miss makes a hit; yet taking a miss is often a mistake. Wattx is UP in HIS Gaammert..—" Willie, is it right to say •my sister has came to school'?" "No ma'am." "Why not?" "Because your sister has went home." A Disco:Jam:into ADDITION.--OOTa :4" Doesn't it make you feel nice for people to remark how well you are getting on?" Merritt: "Yes, unless they add they can't understand it." A CoomEermx.—Young Mr. Dolley (as sounds of a feline misunderstanding float on the'air) : "There seems to be an insurrection amongst the cats to-night." Miss Amy: "Or a mew-tiny." LECTURE ON THE FRENCH REVOLUTION.—"It is impos- sible to imagine the chaos that reigned—confusion and anarchy everywhere. In our more peaceful conditions we cannot even imagine such a state of things." Man at the back of the hail: "Yes, we can, mister. Come alp to our house; we're movin'." A lady, overtaken by a heavy shower of rain, tookfre- 'fuge in a store, where she employed the time in making some purchases. "You seem very quiet to-day," she said to the obliging salesman. "Yes, madam." was the reply. "Just look :at the weather! What respectable lade would venture out of doors on a day like this ? " Mr. Henpeck: "Do Poore, you're a lucky dog. My -wife: says that when your wife loses her temper she -never says a word, but goes to the piano and plays a hymn tune until she cools down. I wish my wife:would •do that." De Poore: "You'd change your mind:after you had paid out as much money as I have,igetting the piano repaired." "No, Charlie," said the young girl sadly, "I cannot be your wife. We are to compatible." -"Compatible r' he exclaimed. "Isn't that the very reason;why—" -"Not in our case. I should probably insist,' from mo- tives of economy, on dispensing with a servant and doing soy own housework, and you would:probably let roe do it, Charlie." ONE WAY OF REASONING.—" Ma, I've an idea that some of the folks in this graveyard haven't gone to heaven." "You don't say! What makes you think they haven't ?" "Because I read it on the tombstones." "No!" "Yes, I did, though. It was carved on ever so many—'Peace to his ashes.' Now, there ain't any ashes 'cept where it's very hot, is there, ma ? " "Why did you delay sending for me until your hus- band was out of :his mind?" inquired a pompous , physician. "Oh, doctor." replied the wife, "while he I was in his right mind he would not let me send for you." "How many deaths ?" asks another doctor,in attendance I at a hospital. "Nine." "Why. I ordered medicine for ten." "Yes, but one would not taketit." One morning, after a heavy fall of snow, a little girl i was standing by the window watching the sleighs go by ' in the street in front. She had never seen the like before, I and, what, with the merry jingling of the bells, she was deeply interested. Presently she turned about, and with a great show of animation invited the other occupants of the room to "Come, quick, an' see de folks doin' by in wockin'-chairs !" THINGS ONE COULD WISH 'TO HAVE EXPRESSED OTHERWISE.—PuzzIed Hostess: "I beg your pardon, Lord Bovril—but will you tell me whether I ought to take your arm, or Prince Sulkytoff's, or the Duke's?" Lord Bovril (Lord Lieutenant of the county) : "Well—a —since you ask me, I must tell you that—a--as her Majesty's representative. I am bound to claim the honour! But I hope that you won't for a moment sup- pose that I'm fool enough—a—to care personally one rap about that sort of thing !"—Harper's Magazine. IDLE TIME NOT IDLY SPENT.-0116 Of the best kinds of recreation is some hobby, whereby we ride or drive out of the ruts of our common life. It is astonishing what an interest may be given to ',even the commonest walk I by the knowledge of the mere rudiments of science. Some, however, have no tastes in that direction. For these the recreative change lies in direct play. Socrates, one of the wisest of men, is said, for variety of recrea- tion, to have ridden a wooden horse. When not in humour for physical exercise, he played upon the lyre, which tuned and tempered his mind. Plato, like his master, was a great believer in recreation, and excelled in all the Grecian exercises. Boileau and Luther were great skittle players. The latter relaxed himself by play- ing on the guitar and the flute, and by turning articles in wood. Voltaire's amusement was private theatricals and marionettes. When Diocletian was petitioned to resume the imperial purple, which he had resigned, he replied to the messengers: "You would not have asked such a thing of me it you saw the fine melons I have now ripening, and the plantations about my' villa that I have made." The idle time of Horace, Virgil, Lord Bacon, Pope, Cowper, and of many other writers was spent not idly but with great benefit to their writing /in gardening. The great engineer, George Stephenson, was troubled by his cucumbers, which would grow crooked; but he had large glass jars constructed, into which he inserted the growing fruit, saying, "I think I have bothered them noo," and then they grew straight Sir Walter Scott was an expert wielder of the axe, and competed with his men at Abbotsford as to the paucity of blovis by which a tree could be brought down. The wood rang ever and anon with lauahter while he shared their labours. Among other colebraied woodmen may :be Mentioned Pitt, Wilberforce, and Mr. Gladstone. Archbishop Matey believed in exercise more than in physic. When he felt out of sorts lie took up his axe and went out to hew away at some panderous trunk. Some good people thought that the Archbishop must be a very cruel master because they saw, one piercingly snowy day, .in his ground, a scantily clothed old 'an CUtting WOOGL They were not a little surprised to find that it was the Archbishop himself. "Who is your doctor?" said someone to Carlyle. "My best doctor," he replied, "is a horse." At Laleham, Dr. Arnold used to leap, bathe, and row with his pupils, and always de- lighted in what he called "a skirmish across country." We never could understand why grown-up men are laughed at if they indulge in play; but even a wise man like Dr. Samuel Clarke was afraid of fools. Once, while exercising himself with a friend in leaping over chairs, he said, " Now;we must stop, for a fool is coming."—The A rgosy.

The Liberals of Brighton are tn aking strenuous efforts to recover the ground they have lost. An active agent has been appointed, well versed organisation and registration work, and he has al- ready made visible improvements. The next thing in hand is a big demonstration, which has been fixed for the 12th of June , Lord Herschell has con- sented to deliver an address on the occasion.

A lady who was present at the presentation of the "album" containing signatures of sympathisers representative of every class in the country which Mrs. Priestley gave to M Pasteur a few clays ago in Paris writes :—Pasteur seemed to grow happier at every moment as the leaves of the wonderful book of signatures were turned over, and when at last it was closed he addressed Lord' Lytton warmly on the muzzling question, telling him that whereas before muzzling was enforced England more than any other country suffered from hydrophobia, it was now of all others the most exempt. He also urged Lord Lytton to make this fact known in England as widely as possible. Lord Lytton promised to do

It is remarkable how completely politics have fallen out of general conversation. If it were not for Africa and Newfoundland there would be no- thing to talk about except the " Frencheries " and the" Sodgeries." On African questions Lord Salis- bury must be somewhat amused to find himself abjured day after day not to surrender an inch of territory to the Germans. There is quite a Jingo feeling creeping up in London; I do not know if it has yet extended to the provinces. Mr. Stanley has already touched the easily susceptible imagina- tion of the club man and the diner out ; and. even journals that profess and call themselves Liberal are quite ready for an annexa- tion of unknown territory, and for a contro- versy with Germany which may involve a serious quarrel. It is wortk stating, therefore, that the negotiations are likely- to be prolonged for ith I indefinite period. I doubt if they Will end much ' earlier than the session. In the meantime both parties are on such good terms that there is a mutual agreement not to prejudice the case by any prema- ture action.

Newfoundland seems to excite even more feeling than Africa in some minds. Sir Charles Dilke has given the hint. In his "Problems of Greater Bri- tain' he comments on the "extraordinary feature' of the French shore, by reason of which a British colony is denied full rights over its own soil. The controversy, he remarks, is one out of which," but for an amount of tact on both sides which cannot be permanently counted upon, war might arise at any time." Sir Charles takes the Newfoundlanders' side of the case, and if he were in office would be negotiating in their favour. With his authority to back them, the friends of the New- foundlanders are now threatening us with an immediate secession of Newfoundland, unless the Foreign office can persuade M. Ribot to take some- thing in exchange for French rights, whether money or territory elsewhere. The threat of seces- sion is ridiculous. Newfoundland csuld not fight France alone, and if an appeal were made to the United States the Americans would only enter into the legal rights against France which we ourselves possess. But there does seem to be some project on foot for compensating the French, and giving the Newfoundlanders that complete control over their cod fisheries and their lobsters which they have never possessed for now nearly two centuries. The idea has not, however, been received with en- thusiasm in Paris, and the negotiations will pro- bably take even longer than those which affect the future of East Africa.

Mr. Gladstone's statement that there has been no I obstruction this session is amply supported by the inexorable logic of figures, as recorded by un- doubted friends of the Government. It is indeed surprising, when we consider that Ministers are supposed to have the confidence of their followers, to find that nevertheless their friends have occupied with speeches 122 hours out of a total of 421 hours of the session, while all the objections of the Opposition have been delivered within the space of 191 hours. Members of the "Unionist" party have, it is admitted, put 402 questions and made 705 speeches, so that if anything is to be said of waste of time the fault must be laid at the door of those who, it might be supposed. would be satis- fied with the voice of Ministers. This view is con= firmed by the proceedings last week, when Mr. Smith was able to secure a certain amount of expedition by the threat of shorter holidays. Then, and not till then, did the Ministerialists observe a discreet measure of silence. While their contribu- tion throughout the session to Whitsuntide was so nearly level with that of the Opposition, it fell to less than one-fourth when the holidays were at stake.

A specialist in dairy products who was sent out last autumn to India to test, examine, and report upon the milk of the various bovine animals in that coun- try has returned this month to England. Anglo- Indians here who are familiar with the nauseous fluid they drank as " milk " in Hindostan will be surprised to hear as the main result of the investi- gation that all the milks of that land are reported to be always as rich as, and mostly richer than, the best English cows' milk in cream and butter yielding qualities The number of dairy beasts in all parts of the country is stated to be incredibly numerous in proportion to the acreage of past ure. With better cattle fodder an enormous yield would be the result. The present average price of butter throughout Bengal and the North-west Provinces seems to be Bd. to 10d. per pound. The expert is quite enthusiastic about the excellence of Indian ghee, derived from clarified buffalo's milk, and used universally for cooking pur- poses. He recommends the introduction of a simi- lar substance into English kitchens. Many of the experiments were conducted under the auspices of Government officials. Special instructions were likewise given to natives in the most approved I methods of butter making, cream separation, and I kindred operations.

Next to Mr. Gladstone, Lord Rosebery is unques- tionably the most popular politician north of the Tweed. He is almost idolised in Edinburgh; his authority is great throughout Scotland. While the Unionists have to struggle against the unpopularity of the Duke of Argyll, who repels the most ardent admirers. Lord Rosebery increases the enthusiasm for Home Rule by his adoption of the cause. There are personal qualities which explain something of his influence : but the speech which he made on co-operation this week gives another hint of the causes of his popular strength. The topic is no longer obscure in any sense, but it is just one of those upop which duller men deliver lugubrious essays. 'They steep themselves in poli- tical economy, and they moan about capital and labour until their audiences are depressed. Lord Rosebery, thsugh he showed a complete acquaint- ance with the subject. was popular and bright. He was, perhaps, a little too enthusiastic. Co-operation I does not necessarily mean all the virtues of which humanity is capable. But his speech to the Co- operative Congress is so flowing and genial that nobody need be at a loss for an explanation of the fact that whenever he attends a public meeting there are loud cries for" Rosebery! Rosebery ! "

There will be held on Saturday next t 14e biggest temperance demonstration ever organised. It will be of greater proportions than the demon- stration of 1888. It has often been said that the temperance party is the best organised party in the country, and on June 7th its leaders are about to show it. For more than a week past committees have been sitting in London, and now organisation is actively going on for the demonstration in Hyde Park, where the Publicans' Pension Bill will be denounced as a Bill has seldom been denounced before. It is not to be either purely or mainly a metrepolitan gathering. Dele- gates from distant provincial towns are to come up, not in singles and couples, but in dozens and hundreds. Indeed, there is talk of running special excursion trains from surrounding towns within a wide area to the metropolis; while those centres which cannot be personally represented, are raining in letters of congratulation and support. Without distinction of party or creed, all reformers are in- vited. One of the most influential contingents will be the Roman Catholics, to whom Cardinal Manning is to address a few words of advice before they march. Support from the advanced wing of the Church of England Temperance Society is pro- mised ; there will be councillors by dozens, and members of Parliament by scores. Possibly the de- monstration may not be so big as the labour demon- stration of last month, but it will be a large affair.

The Prince of Wales considers that 'his own very early emanci?ar- tion from parental control was rather a mis- fortune than otherwise, and in the case of his sons he has steadily set his face against any pre- mature or precocious independence. But now, with a Parliamentary income, a house of his own, and a seat in Parliament, Prince Albert) Victor is fairly launched in public life. He is a remarkably amiable and good-tempered young man, curi- ously free from Royal airs and graces, easily amused, and fonder of a quiet life of simple recreation than of hard work or stirring adven- ture. The next and most momentous step in his career will be his marriage. His friends are very anxious that he should marry Princess Vic- toria of Teok "Princess May," as she is commonly called. She is very pretty, very gracious, a thorough Englishwoman and the daughter of them st popu- lar of all our Englishwoman, ladies. Her degree of relation- ship to the young Duke—second cousin once re- moved—is not near enough to constitute any seri- ous drawback, and if only the young people wish it, and the powers that be consent, it would be impossible to arrange a more suitable or more satis- factory marriage.

The Dukedom of Clarence is derived from the honour of Clare, in Suffolk. The heiress. of Clare married Lionel Plantagenet, who was created Duke of Clarence. The dukedom became extinct on his death in 1388. It was revived by Henry IV. in favour of his son, Thomas Plantagenet, and again became extinct in 1421. It was revived again in favour of George Plantagenet, brother of Edward IV., who, according to Mrs. Markham and other un- impeachable authorities, was drowned in a butt of Malmsey. The dukedom was not again revived until 1789, when it was conferred on Prince William Henry, afterwards King William IV. The title of Avondale is Scotch, and has been several times borne by members of the Royal House of Stuart; and the Earldom of Athlone is an Irish title, not hitherto borne by any Royal person. Thus, as in the creations of all the Queen's sons, the claims of England, Scotland and Ireland are recognised in the Parliamentary style of the ultimate Heir to the Crown.

Thou'rt nought short but a camel, an' two or three monkeys, an' thou'll be set up for life. But I'm noan boun to ha' that thing i' this house, I can tell tho'. Oh. I'm kilt!' cried Sall, I'm kilt!' an' I went to help her; but, just as I wur bendin' down, hoo up we her foot and took me bang between th' een, we sich a welt that sparks flew i' o' directions; an' down I went staggerin', tlehinder- end first, into a mugful o', dough, that stood at th' end o'th' dresser—and there I stuck fast. By this time hoo'd geeten to her feet; and while I war busy, tryin' to wriggle mysel' out o'th' mug, hoo flung an' owd birdcage at mi yed, that wur stonnin' i'th' nook—an' that wur followed we a mugful estarch that coom flush into my face, an' filled my mouth an' een, till I wur as blint as a bat. I knew not where th' dog's londed ; but it took off toward YOr'Shire, an' I've never sin it fro' that day to this; don't think I ever shall—as lung as our Sail's alive. . . Well, when I'd poo'd mysel' out o'th' mug, ',fund our Sall rear% up again th' dresser, strokte her nose, an' tryin' to get her breath ; an' I believe, toth' best o' my remembrance, that I said some words that I never yeard in a chapel—but nowt mention 'em again. THE CORSICAN UPSTART.—The French Revel° lion had not only shocked and horrified the sober. winded folk of Europe—and, we may say, America also—by its atrocities and bloodshed, b tt had brought about a state of things whieli we: to the ruling classes of the Continent and England a standing outrage upon the fundamental pile eiples of society and government. Here was a "Corsican upstart" at the head of France; his Ministers were men risen from the ranks; his code which he rigorously imposed on all the territories which he either conquered or annexed, made all men equal before the law, and rendered an aristocratic government impossible. The walks of life were thrown open to all; any man, no matter how humble his origin, might be an officer of the army, might even become a marshal of France. The spectacle which the empire of Napoleon pre- sented, moreover, was most encouraging to the g towth and spread of the new ideas and the new system. France, Belgium, Holland, the German setates on the Upper Rhine, Italy, had all adopted, to a greater or less extent, the new doctrines, and they were all in a condition of unexampled pros- perity, despite the ware of the last dozen years. The new monarch, too, was plainly a restless scheming, ambitious man. He and his system ought to be overthrown; the • safety of society, the interests of public morals, demanded it, to say nothing of the balance of power, which was great- ly disturbed by the excessive preponderance of France. The state of feeling at this time in Europe was, as respects this subject, wholly differ- ent from that which exists to-day. It has now been found by experience, that these contrasts in the ideas and forms of government existing in contiguous countries do not necessarily, or even generally, lead to war, or even to the introduction into the more conservative countries of the liberal notions of their next neighbours. But in the last years of the last century, and the first years of this, almost everybody in Europe thought different- ly.—Frotu "Some Illustrations of Napoleon and ids Times," by John C. Ropes, in Scribner's Magazine, EINTS TO SWIMMERS.—When the bathing sea- son arrives, remarks a natatorium professor, we'll bear of the usual maximum of drowning cases, and among them, as usual, a fair share of expert swimmers. The chief reason why good swimmers are so often drowned when they are accidentally thrown into the water is because the shock causes them to lose their presence of mind. The loss of presence of mind leads to paralysis of body, or to. Nuch wild exertions as accelerate drowning, in- stead of contributing to preservation. The ability to behave wisely in case of sudden accidents can only be acquired by experience • just as every- thing else has to be acquired.. Hence in some of the European swimming schools, the pupils are taken out boat riding and purpoliely upset, as though it were aucidental. They are also sudden. ly pushed overboard, and subjected to all manner of prepared accidents, so as to accustom them to acting in emergencies. In this way they learn how to behave in case of real aocidente, and are ,protected against the loss of their presence of mind on occasions of danger on the water. They are also taught to have faith in the sustaining power of the water itself. They get to•know that the water will sustain them if they will only render it the least help. A finger laid upon an oar, I or the gunwale of an overturned boat, or a board, or almost any floating substanee„ will sustain the human body in calm water. Persons who have been properly taught, and have acquired the habit of acting with self-possession in the water when the, are upset, do not attempt to climb upon the overturned boat, but simply take hold of it and quietly support themselves. A bout half filled with water, or completely overturned, will sup port as many persons as can get their hands upon the gunwale, if they behave quietly. In a case of accident, a person who understands and acts in accordance with these facts would stand a better chance of being saved, even if he were a poor swimmer, than an expert swimmer would stand who should lose his presence of mind. CHINA and glass are substances which frcquent- ly demand mending in most households ;, the best cement for these substaucea is that sold under the name of diamond cement, which is colourless and resists moisture. It is made by soaking isinghes in water till it is soft and then dissolving it in proof spirit. Add to this a little gum annxioiliac or gallanum and mastic' both dissolved in as little alcohol as possible. When the cement is to be used it must be gently liquefied by placing the phial containing it in boiling water. The phial must be closed with a good cork, not by a glass stopper, as this may become fixed. It is applied to the broken edges by a camel's hair pencil. When the objects are not to be exposed to moist- ure, the white of egg alone, or mixed with finely sifted quicklime, will answer very, well. Shellac dissolved in spirits of wine is, however, better. A very strong cement for earthenware- is- made by boiling slices of skimmed milk cheese with water into a paste, and then grinding . it , with quiekliine in a mortar. "IT will be all over London directly," was Mark's first thought. His second was that Ruth would hear Ond believe. No: she would never believe him to be $ thief, It was impossible,

Yti a short time he had grown more compo,ed, and, with the orderly method of a man of business, he began o make his plans. His first was to send for his brother, but a strange kind of shrinking made him heeitate to do this. He could not tell why, only that Martin did not seem to be the kind of man he could trust in such an emergency. He must have a good solicitor, and, knocking at his cell door, he had a message rent to a gentleman in Lincoln's-inn-fields. In half an hour the messenger was back with the answer that he might have anticipated—" Offices closed!" To get over this difficulty, he sent a telegram to the solicitor's private residence, and once more at down to wait and think of the porter's words. "He evidently believed I was the culprit," said Mark to himself; "and that might easily have hap- pened. But Rlopstock? He would not speak; and evidently was under the same impression. Goad heavens! Am l going mad ?" He would have given anything for the power to calm his excited feelings by walking up and down, but that solace was denied him, and he could only sit and think till his head began to throb. "Who could it have been ?" Wednesday was again a very busy day at Hawarden, the influx of excursionists falling very little short a the

div.head: TrIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 31, 1890.
div.p: TrIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 31, 1890.

largo number which filled the village on Tuesday. One of ti • eireoriions was organised by the Women's Liberal Assoolation of Bradford. tip to Tuesday evening no Iless than 1,500 tickets had been sold for this excursion alone, and the organisers found. it necessary to issue 200 more, an addition which fell considerably below the demand. Two exceptionallylong trains left the Exchange Station, Bradford, at seven o'clock in the morning, and reached Hawarden sbortly after noon. At Barnsley, the division represented by Lord Compton, the lacal Liberal Association had arranged an excursion, and the party , from there numbered about 1,500. They travelled in two trains, and reached Hawarden about noon. From Cardiff a party of 700 to 800 travelled by an excur- sion promoted by the South Wales and Monmouthshire Liberal Federation. Excursions were also run from Derbyshire. Nearly 5,000 people gathered in the park. On the (.terrace an address was presented to Mrs. Glad- stone, from the Bradford Women's Liberal Association, as well as a bouquet otorchids. Mrs.Glaclstone expressed her warmest thanks and Mr. Gladstone then came for- ward, and was received with loud cheering. Be would say this for his countrymen, that though they might have many faults, one of their good qualities was a generous and disinterested regard for the concerns of others. In the address it was stated that it was the cause of Ire- land that called into exiatence the Women's Liberal As- sociation at Bradford. and he rejoiced to'think that in this country the people felt for the wrongs of others as deeply and truly as though they were their own. There could be no more healthy sign, for when as a people they began to show a real sympathy with others less happy than themselves, it was evident that there was some- thing 'like a beginning of deliverance from selfish- ness. He then touched upon the subject of music, and, referring to the singing he had heard from the excur- sionists,maintained that Yorkshire and Wales possessed the musical gift in an extraordinary degree, and could hold their own against any other people in that respect. He urged them to continue to cultivate this excellent gift, which brightened and sweetened life. WELSH LIBERALS AT HAWARDEN. A number of Welsh Liberals, including a deputation from the Carnarvon Boroughs Women's Liberal Associa- tion, visited Hawarden, on Thursday, and presented Mrs. Gladstone with an address. Mr. Lloyd George, and Mr. Thomas Lewis, M.P., accompanied the party. Mrs. Gladstone, in accepting the gift, particu- larly thanked the women 'Liberals for what they had 'done, and said, amid laughter, that women could do a great deal if they only 'kept quiet over it. Mr. Gladstone, who was loudly cheered. referred to the recent victory at Carrrarvon and reminded the elec- tors that in fighting the battle Of Ireland they were also fighting thd battle of Wales. The two were inseparable, and the man would be lacking in common sense who attempted to create anyrivalry between them. 'lreland, Scotland, anctWales hid made up their minds on Home Rule, but' England had taken more time. Now; however. they had got to look forward, and the only :thing that could do them any 'harm would be 'disunion among themselves. He counselled patience and Totlaearance, for it could not be denied that there was a very great and serious competition with regard to different questions vitally affecting the people. Whatever the claims of Wales, Scotland, Yottshire, arid other parts of the kingdom might be, there was one interest that they must all have, and that was the getting of Ireland out of the way. The English :Liberals had now made-up their minds. They weresil marching shoulder to shoulder, and the should be .glad if it pleased the Almighty to let him see the marcb' brought to a final issue, an issue he was confident weld be reached for the great good of the country.

div.head: EIGHT HOURS QUESTION.
div.p: THE EIGHT HOURS QUESTION.

MR. BURNS' REPLY TO4 MR. BBADLAUGH. , Mr. John Burns, in a rejoinder to Mr. Bradlaugh, In the controversy on the compulsory eight hours working day, discusses three objections raised by Mr. Bradlaugh. Upon the first, that foreign competition would ruin onany of our industries, Mr. Burns remarks—" The foreign competition argument was,used from 1802 up to 1878 against the Factory and other ,Acts, and its weik- ness was shown by the doubling of our wealth between 1844 and 1858, when the hours of labour were reduced from fourteen to ten for women and children, and also indirectly for men. And, singular though it may appear Ito some, our danger is not in the foreigner working his 'people long hours and paying them low wages—which the fear of revolution is rendering impossible—but in his going further than England in the direction of shorter hours and better wages, and in doing so, using the same weapon against us that we have used successfully against him. This is strikingly shown by the fact that America with its better conditions, is becoming the successful competitor against all others in the manufacture of machinery, tools, and in other industries." As to the objecticm that the eight hours day would mean reduced wages, Mr. Burns argues:—" The objection is historically untrue, especially so in the the trade be which I belong. Wages are determined to-day, under machine industry and sub-division of labour, not so much by the ability of the men as by the number of competitors in the unemployed labour market, created generally by the excessive hours of those in work. Though we cannot, and do not wish to abolish machinery, we can re- move or palliate the competition by reducing hours. Reduced wages would not follow this action, as the determining factor, the unemployed, would have ,the absorbed ; consequently, a rise in wages would be more probable than a diminution. . • . . The fact is, the absorption of one and a quarter millions of unemployed would create a demand for commodities in the home market, which would more than counter- balance the increased cost of production consequent upon the generally reduced hours." On the third objection raised by Mr. Bradlaugh, that State interference is not necessary or advisable, "except for the purpose of pre- venting injury to life or health, or any matters on which the people are, or reasonably ought to be, able to pro- tect themselves," Mr. Burns observes :—" This seems a remarkable argument from the author of a Truck Act for grown men, who, if Mr. Bradlaugh is right, ought to have been strong enough, through their unions, to pre- vent beer and potatoes being forced upon them by un- scrupulous employers in lieu of wages.'

div.head: NEWFOUNDLA.ND FISHERIES DISPUTE. THE COLONIALS ARMING FOR REPRISALS.
div.p: THE NEWFOUNDLA.ND FISHERIES DISPUTE. THE COLONIALS ARMING FOR REPRISALS.

Great excitement prevails thoughout Newfoundland. The people have been rendered desperate by the last two French outrages. The whole fishing population, ashore and afloat, are arming, and agents are buying arms and ammunition for the crews of the fishing vessels. Unless the British Government rescind the recent arbitration, which gives France territorial rights on the coast, it is believed that the whole colony will rebel against British rule. Great indignation is fett at no attempt being made to chastise Captain Jean Bischell, of the French schooner 'Marie. That vessel in entering port at Basque carried away some fishing nets, and when the owraer went on boaid to claim compensation, he was unceremoniously turned ashore. Legal proceedings were taken, but Captain Bischell failed to answer to the magistrates' summons, and judgment was given against him. A warrant was then issued for the captain's arrest, but when the constable in order to serve it boarded the Marie, he was made prisoner and the schooner sailed away with the captive. The second outrage, which has greatly added to the popular indignation, was perpetrated on the crew of the Newfoundland schooner Advance, which arrived at Bonavista on Monday week after being in collision with a French fishing brig. During the time of contact the crew of the Advance were barbarously treated by the Frenchmen, who beat them off With bars. Several of the crew of the Advance were badly hurt, and the =leis likely to die from the injuries he received. It is thought that hostilities may break out at any moment, as the French men-of-war on the coast do not respect the British flag. It was rumoured on Saturday morning that two British war ships have received sealed orders to proceed at once to the scene of the trouble which is evidently brewing on the Newfoundland coast. It is also reported that H.M.S. Pelican (Commander Riddell), which is at present cruising in the gulf of St. Lawrence, has been ordered to proceed on a similar service. St. John's city is in a state of feverish excitement. A telegram dated Sunday, says—A French war vessel has just entered St. George's Bay, and has landed a force of marines in full campaigning equipment. This step is re- garded by the population as virtually an invasion of British territory. The officer in command Of the French marines has ordered all Newfoundland fishermen to im- mediately cease fishing, tinder the threat of confiscating all nets found upon fishing vessels disobeying this man- date. It is impossible to describe the intense deep- rooted indignation which this last act of French auda- city has excited in the locality. All classes join in con- demning the supineness of the British Government, and even the most patriotic and loyal of the citizens of New- foundland are animated by a sense of discouragement. The British warships which are hourly expected, have not yet reached the scene of this last outrage, and their arrival is anxiously expected in the hope that they will give effect to the Newfoundlanders desire for re- taliation.

div.head: LORD ROSEBERY AND COOPERATION.
div.p: LORD ROSEBERY AND COOPERATION.

Lord Rosebery, presiding at the twenty-second annual congress in Glasgow, on Monday, of the co-operators of Great Britain and Ireland, said he had always wished to be face to face with the citizens of that State within a State which was called the co-operative movement. He took it for granted that the success of the movement was permanent. During twenty-six years their capital amounted to 471 millions, and their profits to 39 million pounds, while the sales increased by two millions each year. Their habits of thrift must have an effect en the State, and the co-operators formed a band which no statesman could ignore who had the interest of the coun- try at heart. Co-operators had got hold of a great and sure principle which would lead them along the path to pi ogress. They had realized certain theories, and they were pushed forward by accumulated capital. They did not go to the State whining for assistance. They only only asked to be allowed to work out their own salva- tion. (Great cheering.) They had in themselves a system of self-government, and he urged them to give local municipal governments the benefit of their expe- rience. Their main principle was one share one vote. That was a principle that he who ran might read. He urged them to move unitedly, as union was their very existence.

div.head: THIEF CAPTURED BY A LADY.
div.p: A THIEF CAPTURED BY A LADY.

A well-educated youth of sixteen, who gave the name of Albert Easton, and was well dressed, was charged at the Marlborough-st. Police Court, London, on Saturday, with stealing jewellery to the Value of £l5, the property of Mr. M'Mahon, a gentleman residing at 185, Piccadilly. Mrs. M'Mahon said that on Friday afternoon she went to her bedroom, and met the prisoner coming out. She said to him, "Well, what do you want here?" He re- plied "I am looking for Mr. Hermann; are these his chambers. I have been waitinghere ten minutes." She told him that no such person lived there, and allowed him to pass down the stairs. On entering her bedroom she missed a diamond ring from a wardrobe. Perceiving the boy running into Sackville-st. she descended and followed. She called out" Stop thief I" and presently a gentleman stopped him and held him till she got up. Then she said to the prisoner "You have been thieving," but he made no reply. She received the prisoner from the gentleman, and holding him by the hand took him to the Police Station in Vine-st. She afterwards missed other articles. The hall door of the premises was always open, so that the prisoner gained an easy access to the rooms above. Detective Humphries said he searched prisoner's pockets and found the missing articles. On being charged with having stolen the property prisoner i said, " All they are worth s about fifteen pence." He was committed for trial. The prisoner, it is said, was recently a member of a choir at a fashionable West-end church, and was educated at a public school in the locality.

div.head: HUSBAND'S REVENGE.
div.p: A HUSBAND'S REVENGE.

The "St. James's Gazette" has the following :—A scene of an extraordinary character was (we are in- formed by the International Press Agency) witnessed in the West End. A gentleman, accompanied by his groom, was driving along the Kensington Road in a dog- cart, and when near Kensington Gardens he suddenly caught sight of a lady and a foreign gentleman strolling along. Uttering an exclamation of surprise, he sprang from the vehicle whip in hand, and, saying, "You scoml- drel, I have found you at last," commenced belabouring the foreigner, who is understood to be a count, about the head and shoulders. The lady screamed, and the assailed man endeavoured to get away, but fast and furious fell the blows, until eventually the count out-distanced his pursuer and escaped down De Vere Gardens. His assail- ant, probably thinking that he had inflicted sufficient punishment, did not pursue him further, and, remount- ing the dogcart, drove away without exchanging a syllable with the trembling lady who stood near by. The count presently rejoined the lady, and the pair drove off in a hansom. It subseqpently transpired that the assail- ant was a gentleman well known in yachting circles and that the lady was his wife. It seems that this gentleman and his wife made the acquaintance of the count some months ago at Monte Carlo, and that they subsequently met in Paris, at which place the count and the lady eloped. This was the first time the outraged husband had seen the man who wronged him, and it is not, under the circumstances, probable that his summary chastise- ment will be made the subject of police court proceedings.

NEVER RETURNED.—It is said that crie out of every four real invalids who go to foreign countries to recover health never return, except as a corpse. Mr. Goschen, replying, to a Blyth c.rrespondent who inquired if it was true that he had threatened resigna- tion if the licensing clauses were abandoned, 'says the rumour is a simple invention from beginning to end. .THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY'S AMENDMENTS.

- - The legislative sub-committee of the Church of Eng- land Temperance Society, acting under the authority of the executive committee, have drawn up a set of amend- ments to the Government's Local Taxation Duties Bill, which they have put into the hands of Sir William Houldsworth, M.P., who has consented to take charge of them in the House of Commons. The following are the chief points dealt with in the society's amendments The operation of the Act is limited to ten years. The following new clauses are added : Nothing in this Act shall affect any power at present possessed by licensing authority to refuse the renewal, removal, or transfer of any license, or confer on any person interrested in a license any new right, privilege, or claim in respect of such license. No transfer or renewal of a license shall be granted after the passing of this Act, except upon production of the excise license for the time being in force for the pre- mises. Clause 6 gives specific power to County Councils to purchase licenses. It begins: "A County Council may enter into such agreement with persons having any inter- est in premises," &c. The words "with persons having any interest in" are expunged, and the word "regard- ing " substituted. The following addition is also made: "Provided that nothing in this Act, or any agreement made thereunder, shall be deemed to recognise or estab- lish any right or claim of any person to receive compen- sation or payment in the event of the non-renewal or extinction of any license under the Licensing Acts, or any Act which may hereafter be passed amending the same." Clause 8 restricts the grant of new on-licenses except in cases of removal. It is amended so as to apply also to off-licenses and to removals. Sub-section 3of the same clause gives power to the justices with the consent of the County Council to grant new licenses owing to increase of population, to be called "conditional licences." To this the following additions are made The applicant shall give and publish notice of his pro- posed application to the County Council for their con- sent, in the same mann i er as he s by law required to give and publish notice of his application to the licensing authority, and the County Council shall not give their consent until the expiration of the period of one month from the date of the application, and shall, before giving such consent, consider all memorials or representations in writing which may be presented to them before the expiration of such period by any residents or ratepayers "in the place." The County Council may give their consent subject to the condition that the applicant shall deliver up for avoidance one or more licenses in force in the county, or subject to such other conditions as they think fit. EXPRESSIONS OF OPINION. Sir Wilfrid Lawson, in a letter to a correspondent, says he hopes and thinks that there are millions of citizens, comprising teetotallers, moderate drinkers, and even ex- cessive drinkers, who will object to the taxes being em- ployed to raise the value of public-house property. Speaking at Tebay, on Wednesday, on the license- compensation question, the Hon. W. Lowther, M.P. said it was "most honest" to assert that the " rate:. payers generally" would have to pay for extinguished licences. The fact was that compensation would be given by an extra tax on alcoholic liquors. The hon. gentleman did not explain how the "ratepayers gene- rally " will escape.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND.

EXCITING SCENES AT A PROCLAIMED MEETING. On Tuesday a meeting was called to greet Mr. John Dillon, Mr. William O'Brien, and several other members of the Irish party, and was proclaimed by a document posted the previous evening, which, like the one which had reference to last Sunday's gathering at Tipperary, announced that the meeting, if held, would be illegal, as it would lead to boycotting and intimidation. Three members for the county Tipperary Messrs. John O'Connor, Thomas Condon, and Harrison—were amongst those who proposed to attend, and they had expressed their determination to address their constituents in defi- ance of the proclamation. This resolve was persisted in, and though no meeting was held in the town itself, two successful gatherings were held within a short distance of it. There was a good deal of batoning, and in one in- stance a crowd which had assembled in the streets of Cashel was dispersed by a charge of hussars. Several people were injured during the day. Cashel is the centre of a large section of the agricul- tural portion of the Smith-Barry estate,and the tenants have joined in the combination against their landlord which was inaugurated in Tipperary. The members of Parliament drove from Tipperary on Monday night. A large forceof police was drafted into the town, and a number of hussars from the Cahir barracks rode over to the scene of the operation on Tuesday morning. It would appear that as Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien were on their way to Cashel the fast horse attached to their vehicle distanced the police wagonettes in pursuit, and when they got to a turn of the road they doubled down a byeway. Shortly afterwards they heard the police cars thundering past, and when the road was clear they did not continue their journey to Cashel, but proceeded to the house of Fattier Ryan, the nari.7ll priest of Clonoulty, where they spent the night. There the plans of action for Tuesday were decided upon. The police arrangements at Cashel were of the most elaberatek.4nd• The forces were under the command of Colonel Tynte and Mr. Shannon, resident magistrates, and they dis- posed of their men with considerable strategic skill, so far as the town was concerned. The disappearance of Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien was undoubtedly a matter of grave apprehension for them, and on the top of the his- toric rock pickets of constables were stationed with binoculars scanning the horizon far and near for the appearance of the meeting. The meeting place arranged for Mr. William O'Brien and Mr. Dillon was Barry's Fort, which is some distance from Cashel. They reached the place without police observation, and were met by a large crowd of people, many of whom were Mr. Smith-Barry's tenants. Father Ryan presided.—Mr. Dillon,in the course of a speech, said this was not the first time that the nationality or religion of Ireland had been driven to take refuge on the hill- sides. The combination of the tenants could not be conquered so long as they had the support of the priests and the people of Tipperary, headed by their Archbishop and the people of Ireland, as was proved by the enorm- ous sum collected for the Tenants' Defence Fund.—Mr. William O'Brien, M.P, who also addressed tha meeting, said that that they were prepared for a long and bitter struggle, but they were not doubtful of the result. The meeting terminated without the appearance of the police. The car conveying the speakers moved on to- wards the town. A crowd had collected about midway between Barry's Fort and Cashel, and a halt was made. A second meeting was in progess when the police arrived and dispersed it with batons. Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien then drove on to Cashel. When they arrived there were numbers of people in the streets, and when the hon. gentlemen were recognised crowds gathered around their car. There was great cheering and excite- ment, and the crowd about the vehicle was growing every moment. At the market-house the police charged the crowd with drawn batons. Mr. William O'Brien's voice could be heard above the tumult protesting against this attack upon a peaceful crowd. The cavalry rode down upon the people, but did not use their sabres. Much damage, however, was done by the biltons, and broken heads were found to be plentiful when all was over, amongst the wounded being several women. The injured people were attended by the local medical man, Dr. Cusack. No further attempt was made to hold a meeting. NEW KNIGHT OF ST. PATRICK. His Excellency the terd Lieutenant, as the Grand Master of the Order of St. Patrick, on Saturday presided over a Chapter of the Knights in St. Patrick's Hall, Dub- lin Castle, The Marquis of Drogheda, the Earl of Carys- fort, Lord Monteagle, and the Earle of Erne, Knights Companion, were present, and the Earl of Kilmorey was invested as Knight of St. Patrick.

SHOCKING MURDER BY A FATHER. A Londonderry correspondent telegraphs that a terri- ble tragedy is reported from Donegal. At a place called Commons, near Donegal, early on Sunday morning, an old man named Daniel McCormack battered out his son's brains with a pair of tongs. The son was lying ill with brain fever, and the father, who is believed to he insane, murdered the lad under the delusion that there was some evil spirit about the house. The old man wa.s ar- rested.

CONVICTION UNDER THE CRIMES ACT. . At Waterford, on Monday, before Messrs. Considine and Irwin, R.M.'s, three charges were heard against Mr. H. D. Fisher, printer and publisher of the " Munster Ex- press," for intimidation, by the publication of reports. The counsel for the defence relied on the judgment of the court of Queen's Bench and other judges, in cases in which the printer and publisher was not the responsible editor. Mr. Considine said as regarded the first two charges they were dismissed without prejudice, hut on the third, the defendant having sold papers containing articles condemning la.ndgra hhers, they must convict with a sentence of three months' imprisonment. The defend- ant appealed, having now three appeals pending, THE IRISH TENANTS DEFENCE FUND. The Archbishop of Dublin, in sending a cheque for £5O to the Irish Tenants' Defence Fund, points out that it has reached £60,000. This money, he beijeve.s, represents the most ,generous effort as yet made by the pcopleof Ireland, and by those who sympathise with them at home and abroad, and the assertion of the fundamental principle of Christian morality that the property of the poorest and the most oppressed tenantry- in Ireland is as sacred as the property of the richest and most exacting land- lord.

SIXTEEN YEARS' IMPRISONMENT THOUGH INNOCENT.

In the depatches which were landed at Liverpool on Saturday from New York, a case was reported of an innocent man who had just been released after serving sixteen years in the penitentiary for a crime of which he was innocent. The man, whose name is William Star-- nicker, was arrested on suspicion of murdering Henry Chance, in Burke county. Starnicker had just previ- ously had some difference with Chance. He protested his innocence, but was nevertheless convicted and sen- tenced for life. About a fortnight ago, a man named Crane died in Burke county, and on his death bed con- fessed that the evidence he gave against Starnicker was false. It was on the evidence of Crane that Starnicker was really convicted. After a thorough inquiry into the confession by Governor Gordon, the condemned man.. was liberated. The poor fellow said no one could realize his feelings on being convicted for the crime, when he knew he was innocent. For most of the time Starnicker had been working in the mines and quarries belonging to. the penitentiary. Although convicted and imprisoned for sixteen years, he was grateful that the matter had been cleared up and himself proved innocent.

div.head: s;',IIIOLTS FIRE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: s;',IIIOLTS FIRE AT WARRINGTON.

A serious fire broke out shortly before 11 o'clock on Saturday nigh* in a central and populous part of on the premises of Warrington that is ,to Ply and Son, eurriera and Messrs. Thomas Whittle' ke- leather merchants, Buttermatst. The fire watt : :l! first detected by a son of the suerintendent of the fire brigade, who, while walking up the street,, detected through a window the brealci:ig out of the, flames. He at once gave the alarin,and the tire brigade, under Superintendent Turner, was soon on the spet, but not before the flames had got a good 11)1d of the pre-, mises. An ample supply of water was obtained, but the, firemen had some difficulty with the hydrant at the corner of Scotland-road. Owing to the constant traffic over it the plate had become so firmly fixed that for a while it resisted all efforts to move it. When, however, the firemen had got their hose in full play they worked with a will, and it was not long before the effect was seen in the gradual suppression of the outbreak. Ad-. joining Messrs. Whittle's premises is a private house, some of the occupants of which were retiring for the night when the fire was discovered. The flames litery quickly obtained a hold of the building, and shot out in fierce blasts half-way across the street. Residents , of neighbouring houses, fearing the spread of the- fire, took the precaution to remove the more valuable of their goods to places of safety. The brigade worked bravely, although the movements of the men were greatly hampered by the presence of an immense concourse of spectators, who asembled so quickly and in such numbers that the police were powerless to cope with them. When the fire was at its height the tooting. of a horn announced the approach of the mail coacis from Manchester. With commendable forethought the police intercepted the vehicle. and sent it round by way of Mersey-st. The fire, which seems to have originated, from what cause is unknown, in the shop, spread to the back of the premises, and upwards to the second and ' top storeys. In little more than an hourand a half from the time of the outbreak the. firemen had obtained the mastery, and succeeded in extinguishing the fire. Several members of the brigade were left in charge until morn- ing; and the necessity for this was shown when some hours afterwards flames broke out afresh in the upper portion of the building. They were soon subdued, and no further danger was experienced. None of the adjoin- ing property was touched. Had the fire spread to the premises of Mr. Chorley, marine store dealer, the con- sequences would undoubtedly have been much more serious. The damage, which is very considerable, is covered by insurance. One or two feats of prowess were made by the firemen during the progress of the con- flagration. one of them doing great execution with his axe, and another, making a risky ascent to the roof of the building.

Mr. Gladstone THE speech which Mr. GLADSTONE at made at Howarden, on Monday, to Hawarden. the Liberals from Bristol, isia trum- pet call to, duty. It shows that the great leader of the Liberal party is ardent as ever in the cause of progress, and eager to grapple with his oppo- nents, whoever they may be. Mr. GLADSTONE has a wonderful capacity for adapting himself to his audience. Thern speech is not such a one as would, have been made to the members of the House of Commons, for. in addressing the House it is assumed, in most cases, that they. are in possession of the main facts of the case, and that the chief.point is to drive home arguments upon them. In speaking to a mixed assembly, such as that which he addressed on Monday, the Liberal chief is as a rule careful to begin at the &ginning, ' so .that his audience may not, be at a loss in the close reasoning which always follows upon ,his statement of the case. It thus happens that he is invariably able, by appealing to the common- ;sense and moral instincts of the people, to bring them in close sympathy with what he says, And raise them to. his high plane of thought. ,Nothing could be. better, for instance, than the way in which. Mr. GLADSTONE re-stated the facts of the Mitchelstown Massacre, and thus brushed aside, the cobweb fallacies of the Irish Secretary and the "Daily Telegraph." He singled out the . " Telegraph " in a way which everybody but ' the Editor of the " Telegraph " will regard as exceedingly happy, by describing it as an organ "which is extremely loyal to every principle opposed to Liberalism." The London organ of " alantingdicular "neutrality seems to have made an awful hash of it in defending the action of. the police at Mitchelstown. It repeated the exploded contention with regard to the men who were killed, by saying that "had they remained at their places they could not have been shot, because we have no Irish crooked muskets, famous for. shooting round corners." Mr. BALFOUR was the first,, we believe, to put forward the suggestion that thethree men who werenaassacred lost their lives because they had left the meeting at the Market- place„ and followed and atoned the police on their retreat to the barracks. This puzzle about shoot, ingeround the corner was considered very funny. until the answer was given. The answer was„to use Mr. GLADSTONHS words, "that from the window where„ the police fired a photo was made of the spot where one of these three men fell in the Market- place, and from the spot where the man fell in the Market-place a photo was. also made of the window ' from which the police fired." "You see now," he added, "the brazen-faced. audacity with which I the. statements are made The "brazen-faced. audacity of the " Telegraph " is in this instance coupled with arrant stupidity, for it ought to have known that as far back as the great Liberal. demonstration in Birmingham, in 1888, Mr. GLAD- ' STONE gave the lie to the round-the-corner theory hy, producing the photograph, and remarking that the photograph, at any rate, could not lie. It is. 'well that the people of. this country should be 'reminded again and again that the three men who. 'ware "wantonly, wickedly, ruthlessly shot" at Mitchelstown were sraughtered whilst attending a legal and peaceful meeting, and that it was • the police who acted illegally, and were.. guilty of misconduct and disorder. It should be remembered. that the meeting was not a, proclaimed one, that it was. held in the public ql2are, in the usual way, and. that the police had no more right to try and force a way through, it to the platform than any. other body of men would have, to attain their own ends. But the shameful feature of the whole shameful business is that one of the constables who was haiured whilst engaged in an illegal act haa been, liberally compensated, whilst sato the three men who were killed.," there has been no inquiry and no, attempt in any shape at redress." Mitchelstownia the Peterloo oflreland, and at the next election the cry must, be— " Remember MitcheLstown.l" After, exposing the weak points of the Irish Land. Bill, Mr. GLADSTONE, proceeded to ,deal at some, length with whatheg aptly described as "The Public-house Endowmeatßill." We commend his temperate and closely-reasoned observations as to the probable effect of the. Bill to those, who have hitherto been favourably disposed towards it. If. they look at the matter dispassionately, and on all sides, they will see. that the Government Bill, in- stead of proving, as iaclaimed for it,. an aid to the temperance cause,, will be the greatest hindrance to that cause which has been seengiaa this genera- tion. To put, as, Mr. GemisroN3k,says, " en.! ormous money weight upon every transaction con-. 'meted with the reduction of thenumber of public- houses, or with the withdrawal of licenses, is; to. erect a new and terrible impedEment in the, way of every temperance reform.!" It may seem to some that a matter of £350,0a0 a year, which the Government propose to hand over to,the County Councils with the object a buying out licenses,, cannot be regarded as an "enormous money weight," but as to this it must be remembered that if the County Councils are to be limited to this small sum it means that any action they may take will be ridiculously inadequate. It has been computed that it would take 700 years to extin- guish all the licenses with this sum of 4:350,000 a year, but if half only of the licenses were to be bought up, it will be seen how preposterous it is to undertake a task which could not be completed in less than 350 years. The Government,to do them justice, do not contemplate anything so 'absurd. What they know is that if they can, by this Public-house Endowment Bill, get in the thin end of the wedge of compensation, it will have to be driven home by the ratepayers and taxpayers at a cost of millions of money. 'The assumption is that the £350,000 a year would soon be supplemented by many other hundreds of thouaands a year. In

this way the great brewers, like insatiableVompireei would suck the life blood of the people. if their claim was a jast ono, founded upon reason and pro' ceclent, it would be our duty to meet it, however burdensome it might prove. But it is not just,---' it is not reasonable; for the highest courts of the land have determined that the 14. w doss not recor nise • any such thing at a vested interest in e license. It is true that the trade," in so far as licenses have as a rule been renewed from year to year, have enjoyed what may be looked upon as monopoly, and how they have profited by that monopoly is shown by the' enormous fortunes which such men as Sir GILBEVZ GRBENALIr have realised in a comparatively short space of time. A claim for compensation might much more reason- ably be set up on behalf of the tens of thousands, of sufferers frock what Lord RarinoLmi Caunouttg, forcibly described as "a destructive, and deviliski traffic." " Thetrade" has no clairn.for compensa' tion, as the law at present stands, and as it. 110 stood for hundreds of years, and it is for the publie to take care that no claim is set up by the passing of the mischievous Bill which is at present before' the House of Commons. There is a talk, at times/. of mandates, but there has been no mandate froze the people to endow the liquor traffic.. On Ole' contrary, two years ago the electors made it clear ' that they would be party to no such monstrouS' proposal, and if they will only make themselves' heard by ineeting,upon meeting, as they did then, • they will even ,yet compel the Governrnent•to awignominious retreat, as they did in 1888:,

WHITSUNTIDE AT WIDNES. The people of Widnes took full advantage of the holi- day on Monday, to visitfairer and brighter scenes than the prevailing grey and red of the chemical metropolis, and the railway officials at both stations had a very busy time of it. In the early hours 600 persons departed from the London and North-Western Railway Station for Llandudno by the excursion arranged by the Young Men's Society of St. Mary's Catholic Chapel ; and in the course of the day no fewer than 1,000 passengers were booked for Liverpool. The Brighton of the North, Blackpool, secured 300 trippers, and the gaieties of Belle Vue ,in- duced 400 to travel to Manchester. From the Central Station an excursion, organized by St. Bedes Catholic Chapel, conveyel 600 to Southport, and a similar number Proceeded to the same destination by the ordinary trains. 500 went n search ot pleasures to Liverpool and a simi- lar number travelled to Belle Vue. There were a consi- derable number of passengers booked to other pleasure resorts. The total number of passengers who departed during the day was over 3,000. On both lines the traffic was unprecedented, but it was disposed of with- out a hitch. FRODSHAM POLICE NEWS. _ -

He was later on set at libuty.—Fined 2s. 6d. and 4s. costs.— Mary Worrall, near Bradley Mill, Frodsham, was sum- moned for assaulting Samuel Moss, on April 22nd. SMASHING A BOTTLE ON A MAN'S HEAD AT RUNCORN. Before Dr. Steele, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, Thomas O'Brien, a ship canal labourer, was charged with unlawfully wounding John Hurley, a labourer, who lives at 20, Canal-st. It was alleged that between six and seven o'clock on the previous night Hurley was at the bar of the Barley Mow Hotel, Church-st., talking to M. Hassey, shoemaker, of Cooper-st, when the prisoner entered, and listened to their conversation for some time. He then took from the counter a whiskey bottle containing, water and walking to Hurley, struck him a heavy blow. The bottle smashed in pieces, oneof the frag- ments breaking the glass panel of a.door three yards away. The prisoner, who was sober, then quietly walked out of the Hotel, but Hurley, although he was bleeding pro- fusely from the wounds on his head, followed him and gave him into custody of P.C. Ratcliffe. The prisoner when charged with the offence, said "I know he accuses me of it; he struck me with a glass ; what I did was in self-defence." Hurley was taken to the surgery of Dr. McDougall, and Dr. Clifford dressed his wounds. Dr. Clifford informed the magistrates that the man had five wounds on his head, one of which was an inch long and half-an inch deep. The other were also half-an-inch deep.—The prisoner was committed to the Assizes for trial.

A WIDNES LAWYER AND Hts TIME. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, when the magistrates were about to hear several School Board summonses from Ditton, Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, said his case was an adjourned summons taken out long before the School Board summonses, and he felt ag- grieved that one must wait until several little cases had been disposed of, according to Mr. Lewin's whim. His time had a certain value to himself, and a value to the Court. In other courts it was a custom to take sum- monses according to the date of issue. Mr. Lewin (magistrates' clerk) said the business was conducted quite in order. Mr. Rideal (solicitor), rose to address the Bench, but Mr. Knowles excitedly, objected to him speaking, stating he did not often appear in that Court. Mr. Knowles persisted in interrupting Mr. Rideal, who asked Mr. Knowles if he knew how to behave him- self to do so.—Mr. Rideal : In my. experience— Mr. Knowles: We don't wish to know anything about your experience.—Mr. Brock : Will you allow Mr. Rideal to proceed.—Mr. Knowles : As you please, sir.—Mr. Rideal said this was the first time he had heard a com- plaint as to the business of the Court —Mr. Knowles made another speech, in which he was interrupted by Mr. Brock, who said : lam afraid you are wasting the time both to us and to you.—Mr. Lewin : We always take cases in their order. Mr. Knowles was not present when his case was called on.—Mr. Knowles said he was waiting until the magistrates said whether they would hear his case before or after these school attendance cases.—Mr. Brock : Let the business proceed.—Mr. Knowles then resumed his seat. THE CHESHIRE FRUIT CROPS. - - -

It is stated that it was many years since the fruit trees of Cheshire were so seriously affected by caterpillers. In the BelBol district there will be little fruit of spy description, the apple, pear, and gooseberry trees especially being affected. The disappointment among market gardeners is all the keener as therp, was a magniticent show of bloom.

div.head: MILK AS A SPRRADER OF DISEASi.
div.p: MILK AS A SPRRADER OF DISEASi.

Dr. Fox, medical officer for Mid-Cheshire; told the Altrincham Union tura Sanitary Authority, on Wednesday, not to be alarmed by the assertion re- cently made that milk was one of the means of spreading diptheria. He had investigated hundreds of cases of diptheria, and in none had he been able to trace the infection to the milk supply. Dr. Fox gave an emphatic warning to "the aristocracy and gentry "in regard to the sanitary state of their houses. SUMMER FA9HIONS, now showing at J. Ss W. DUTTON', Sankey-st., Warrington.—Ada. ALLEGED PERJURY AT ST. HELENS. At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Friday, John Corrigan, a collier, of Parr, was brought up on a charge or committing wilful and corrupt perjury at the police court on the previous Monday. On that day a collier named Norman was summoned for being drunk on the afternoon of Sunday, the 11th inst. Norman pleaded not guilty, and called the prisoner Corrigan as a witness. Corrigan was sworn, and he gave evidence that he and Norman were at Billinge and Pemberton all day. The case against Norman was dismissed, but it was after- wards found that Corrigan's evidence was entirely lse,and he was apprehended on the charge of com- mitting perjury. In reply to the charge, he said he had drink in him when he gave the evidence, and Norman told him to say what he had done. The Bench committed Corrigan for trial at the Assizes, and admitted him to bail, himself in the sum of £3O, and two sureties of £l5 each,
TRAVELLIN,4 TRUNKS.—Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge- at.. Warrington. IRON AND STEEL PRICES.

A more favourable result than was generally expected has followed the examination of the books of leading firms in the north of England and the midlands to ascertain the average selling prices of iron during March and April in those two trade centres respectively. According to the ascertain- ment of the accountant to the North of England manufactured Iron Trade Board of Conciliation and Arbitration, the net average price of rails, plates, bars, and angles increased from £6 128.2.39 d. in January and February to £6 163. 513 d. in March and April. This is an improvement of 4s. 3d. per ton upon the period above named: The account- ants to the Midland Iron and Steel Trades Wages Board have declared the average aching price in the midlands to be ..e8 4s. 11d., or an advance of 63. 7d. per ton upon January and February. The midland average price is always considerably high- er than that of the north of England, because in the former case descriptions of iron are included which are not admitted in the latter. The disparity in the selling prices, therefore, shows nothing as to the course of trade. In both districts these an- nouncements have carried with them an advance in wages of 3d. per ton to puddlers, and 24 per cent. to millmen.—lron.

SUDDEN DEATH AT A ST. HELENS HOTEL. On Tuesday morning, Mr. John H. Kearne, of the firm of Messrs. Kearne, Rawlinson, and Co., Bold Manure Works, St. Helens Junction, was found dead in bed at the White Hart Hotel, Church-st., St. Helens. Mr. Kearne, who resided at St. Michael's House, Micklehead Green. near Rainhill, about ten o'clock on the Monday engaged a bedroom. He re- tired about eleven o'clock, and asked to be called early. At seven o'clock next morning Mr. George Ripley, proprietor, knocked at the bedroom door, and called out, "Mr. Kearne, it's gone seven." lie received no aoswer, and entered the room, where- upon he found the deceased lying on the bed. The body was just warm, and Dr. Jackson, assistant to Dr. Gaskell, a few doors away, was immediately called. On his arrival, however, he pronounced life to be extinct. The deceased had on a portion of his clothing, and the bedclothes were scarcely ruffled. It is stated that for some considerable time past he has suffered from heart disease, and death had ap- parently resulted from that affection. He was about 60 years of age. The circumstances were re- ported to the Coroner, Mr. S. Brighouse, who, upon the receipt of a certificate from Dr. E. Casey, of Sutton, that deceased had suffered from heart disease and bronchitis, decided that it was not necessary to hold an inquest. Mr. W. J. Dixon, funeral undertaker, St. Helens, has been entrusted with the interment arrangements. The funeral will take place to-day (Friday), at Birkdale Ceme- tery. TEE REV. C. F. Map.

The Rev. C. F. Aked, pastor of St. Helens (Park- rd.) and Earlestown Baptist Churches), has been invited to become the minister of the Pembroke Bap:Ast Church, Liverpool, the pulpit of which is vacant by the removal of the Rev. W. Pratt, M.A., to Jamaica. Pembroke Chapel is a large edifice in Pernbroke-place, one of the busiest parts of Liver- pool, and is memorable as the scene of the life-long ministry of Dr. Birrell, whose son, Mr. Augustine Birrell, is now M.P. for West Fife. The Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., the leader of the Baptist Forward Movement in London, has also held the pastorate of this church. Mr. Aked entered upon the ministry. at St. Melens and Earlestown about two years ago, and since then there has been a marked increased activity at each place of worship. According to the practise of the Baptist denomination there is no I appeal to an outside authority, but the decision as I to the invitatation rests entirely with Mi. Aked. He has not yet signified his inteution one way or the other. The Manchester' Guardian" says that the im- portant Pembroke Church,once the Premier Baptist Church in Liverpool, has seen many reverses since the long pastorate of the Rev. C. M. Birrell, father of Mr. A. Birrall, M.P., author of " Obiter Dicta,' but, in spite of the changed surroundings of the ichapel, it is confidently hoped, that if Mr. • Aked sees his way to accept the pastorate, he may be able to restore in some measure its former prosperity.

AN EXTRAORDINARY RAILWAY FIRE AT EARLESTOWN. . .

An extraordinary—fire,-Which. -occasioned the delay of two passenger trains, occurred near Earlestown railway station, on Saturday night. The London and North-Western Railway Company's main line between Manchester and Liverpool passes through Earlestown, and near the Viaduct Wagon Works the line is carried through the Sankey Valley by nine immense brick arches, known for many miles around as "The Nine Arches." A goods train was crossing the arches about ten o'clock on Saturday night, when the driver of the engine saw that the wood sleepers and beams below the lines were on fire. He immwiiately reported the circum- stance at Earlestown railway, station, and fore- man William Naylor at once hurried to -the spot. Naylor then reported the matter to Mr. Young, the stationthaster, who gave orders for the Viaduct works fire brigade to be called out. The electric bells were rung, and with considerable promptituch the fire brigade responded. Under the directions of Mr. F. Harwood, manager, the hose pipes were laid to the scene of the fire. In the meantime Mr. Young took one of the locomotives to the spot, and a plentiful supply of water being at hand the flames were extinguished. During these operations the 10.5 passenger train from Liverpool to Manchester, and the 10.10 passenger train from Warrington to Liverpool were each delayed for half an hour. It is supposed that some hot cinders from p&sing engines set ire to the dry woodwork of the bridge. Fortunately the outbreak was dis- covered at an early period or the consequences might have been of a more serious character.
