DRUNK ON " POP " AT WIDNES. A TRAP FOR YOUNG MEN..

Herbert Cook and James Hill, youths about 18 years of age, who reside in Derby-road, Farnworth, were summoned before Mr. Brock, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly on the 18th inst. On the afternoon of the date mentioned P.C. Cummings found the defendants asleep on the roadside in Gorsey-lane. He roused them up, and then dis- covered that they were both very drunk. Hill made use of such violent language that the constable was about to take him into custody, when P.C. Strickland appeared on the scene and had ,them taken home. Cook said they had o..ty had three glasses of "tonic beer, and if that would make them drunk it would make anybody drunk." The defendints informed his Worship that they had only been drinking 66 pop."—Mr. Brock said he happened to know that the defendants did get drunk by drinking what was known as unfer- mented beer; what was commonly known as "herb beer;" but at the same time they were drunk, and that was an offence, and they would have to take the conse- quences. The case would be met by the payment of costs, 7s. ed. He must say that those who sold this herb beer under the plea that it was not ietoxicating were doing a very wrong thing, and if they were brought there and he had anything to do with the case, he should punish them to the utmost extent of the law.—Superin- teudent Noblett said he would make inquiries into this matter.—Mr. Brock: It is simply entrapping young fellows into drinking intoxicating beverages which they would not do.—Each defendant paid the costs.

div.head: LANCASHIRE HUSSARS AT SOUTHPORT.
div.p: LANCASHIRE HUSSARS AT SOUTHPORT.

On Saturday, the Lancashire Hussars entered upon their annual week's training at Southport. The St. Helens and Newton troops of the regiment assembled at their respective headquarters, and proceeded to Ormskirk, where they joined the other detachments and marched to Southport. They were under the command of Colonel the Earl of Lathom. On Monday the regiment commenced their training with a number of heavy drills, including some diffi- cult movements, on the Birkdale foreshore. During the movements the commanding officer fell from his horse, but quickly remounted without having received injury. The band performed selections of music on the promenade in front of the Victoria Hotel, under the direction of Bandmaster Batley, the Earl of Lathom and other officers of the regi- ment being present. The men resumed their drills on Tuesday morning on the Birkdale foreshore. The annual sword competition for the troop and regi- mental prizes given by officers took place on Wed- nesday afternoon, at the conclusion of the drill on the shore. Sergeant-Major Afeates, of the 9th Lancers, officiated as judge. The competition re- sulted as follows ;-c-A Troop (Ash ton-in-Makerfield) : 1, Private Unsworth ;2, Private Knowles; 3, Quar- termasteilGlover. B Troop (St. Helens and Moss Bank) : 1, Sergeant Glover; 2, Corporal Littler; 3 Corporal Eddleston. C Troop (Newton and Liver- pool) : 1, Corporal Squat.); 2, Quartermaster Howard; 3, Sergeant Abbott. ,nD Troop (Ormildrk and Lathom): -1, Sergeant Blundell ; 2, Sergeant Wells ;3, Stopforth. The regimental prize was won, after a keen contest. by Serg ,ant Glover, of B Troop. Special prizes were gut it by Sir Humphrey de Trafford for competition among members of C Troop who had never previously won a prize, with the following result:-1, Private Halsall ; 2, Private Swann; 3, Private Jackson. A VIOLENT YOUNG SAILOR AT RUNCORN, Before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Thomas, at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, a youth named William Hunter, an apprentice on board the schooner Victor, of Banff, was charged with using threats towards his captain, William Laverton. On the previous night, shortly after eleven o'clock,Captain Laverton and the master of another vessel were on the way to their respective ships when they were overtaken by the prisoner, who was staggering along in a drunken condition. On arriving at the " Victor," Cap- tain Laverton told the prisoner to get aboard, and the latter replied that he would go aboard when he liked, and walked away. Later, when the prisoner came on board, the Captain asked him why he had been on shore without leave and why he had insulted him. The pris- oner replied that he was as good a man as the Captain and that he would go ashore who, he wanted. The Captain pushed him towards the forecastle when the prisoner closed with him and they struggled together. The prisoner, who "seemed to be mad," drew a large clasp knife and shouted " I'll knife you," but before he could do any harm the mate, Alexamier Steel, had seized his wrists and disarmed him. The prisAner said he was not that drunk but he could take care of himself, and he only drew the knife because the skipper kept striking him. It was not the first time he had been abused on that ship by the captain. On Sunday morn- ing he was reading a paper in his bunk, when the skipper's brother asked him to peel some potatoes. He replied that he was reading an interesting story, and the skipper's brother said the story could wait, and threw a canful of water on his bed.—Captain Laverton said the prisoner was apprenticed by the owners twelve months ago, and he had had a lot of trouble with him. On one occasion he ran away with some money, but he captured him at the railway station.—Mr. Brundrit gave the pri- soner a severe lecturing, and said it was unwarrantable to draw a knife under any circumstances. He would be bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each, or in default 14 days. —As he had no sureties, he was committed to gaol.
RUNCORN SUNDAY SCHOOLS AND COMPEN- SATION TO PUBLICANS.

After the united procession of Nouccnformist and Catholic Sunday schools at Runcorn, on Whit Mon- day, and while the children were enjoying them- selves in games, ctc., in the field provided fur the purpose, the officers, teachers, and elder scholars of the various schools, held a meeting to consider the compensation clauses of the Local Taxation Act of the Government. The Rev. H. Burson, superinten- dant Wesleyan minister, conducted the proceedings, and he was supported on the platform by the Revs. G. Thompson, C. Finch, J. Simpson, and J. D. Bray, Messrs. John Simpson, James Pritchard, and G. Mar- shall. Mr. John Holford led the assembly in singing ", All people that on earth do dwell," and then Mr. Bur- son explained that they had been called from the plea- sures of the afternoon tc consider a most urgent matter. As they were awarethere was at this moment before the House of Commons a Bill which contained clauses to the effect that if the ratepayers found a public-house a nuisance, a public-house.too many, a public-house that was a death trap, and desired to close it, the brewer or publican should be compensated for having that nuis- ance lifted out of the way. In the opinion of a ,great many in that audience, and of all on the platform and nine4enths of the young people on that field, that pro- position did not commend] tself to thpircommonsense, and to their consciences, (hear, hear), and hence a resolution was to be submitted so that they might add their solemn and united protest against the proposed compensation clauses. (Applause.)—Mr. John Simpson proposed "That this Assembly of Sunday School officers and teachers, re- presenting the whole of the Nonconformist and Catholic Schools of Runcorn, whilst gladly welcoming any attempt to lessen the number of public-houses in our midst strongly protests against any compensation being made. to a trade which offers so many temptations, and is such a serious hindrance to the progress of religion and morality, especially amongst the youth of our land ; and earnestly calls upon all members of Parliament to give. such proposal their most strenuous tloptisition." Mr. Simpson said he considered it a great honour to propose this resolution, which was not in any sense of the word a party question. Men of all parties, and of all classes ; ministers and members of the Church of England. and of the different Nonconformist bod ies, were united in opposing the principle of compensation to publicans, as they did I two years ogo. when they succeeded in compelling the I Galo:rninent to drop the ;till which they had hn,llT.ht for ward. div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUN CORN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUN CORN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The annual procession of scholars passed off very pleasantly on Monday. The weather was very bright and warm, and the children in their new summer frocks, or old ones tastefully done lip, formed a pretty picture as they walked through the streets. As an evidence of the hold that Noncon- for nity has in the town, it may be mentioned that those in the united procession numbed twice as many as those who paraded under the banner of the Established Church. Observed an old man who had watched the pro- cession, and who evidently.posseseed a knowledge of the seamy side of the world, " Its a pretty sight, but it's sad to think that in hundreds of cases, the charming little dresses will he put away and won't see the light of day until another Whit Monday is approaching." He meant, of course, that they would be put on a shelf at" my uncle's," and the manner in which the pawnbrokers' shops were besieged on Wednesday morning added conviction to his words. The pawnbrokers paid out hundreds of pounds on that day, and as one who does a large business re- marked, it was probable that the great majority of the bundles brought in would lie on his shelves until another Whitsuntide drew nigh. There need not be a moral added to the tale. _

What a pity it is, and what is more important, what a loss it is to the public of Runcorn, that there is no competition in railway traffic in the town. The London and North-Western Railway Co. have a monopoly in Runcorn, and like the rest of monopolists, they demand their full pound of flesh and take it. On Tuesday, through the enterprise of the Liberal Club, about 1,200 peqple were enabled to journey to the most charming of Welsh watering places for the sum of 35,, and nearly as large a number had to pay the sum of 2s. 6d. for travell- ing the short distance of 13 miles to Liverpool. In common fairness, considering that it was a working folks holiday, the company might have offered the inducement of a one and sixpenny fare like they do in the pantomime season,and it is not exaggerating to state that had that inducement been given, the increased number of persons who would have travelled to the Seaport City would have swelled the receipts beyond the large amount they must have totalled on Tuesday. Perhaps a selfish consider- ation of this kind may have weight with the head office.

_ A Macclesfield newspaper, where Superintendent Large was for some time in command of the police, thus refers to the inquiry into the administration of the Cheshire police :—" Mr. Slater Lewis probably likes it, yet he is raising a whole host of unbelievers in his case against the police, not only by the method in which he has conducted himself at the inquiry now going on, but by the random charges which he makes. At the sitting on Saturday he imputed the payment of a bribe of £lOO by Superin- tendent Large, late of Macclesfield, to the late Chief Constable for pro Motion, and that accusation was indignantly denied. Besides, Mr. Lewis was mean enough to drag a petty woman's quarrel into the inquiry, as if that was a matter which would affect the control of the police. Even if it had done so, which was scornfully repudiated by both the Chief Constable and Superintendent Large, all the con- solation these officials received from Mr. Slater Lewis is that he is giving them an opportunity of denying certain rumours. It is greatly to be de- plored that the Committee should have made such a long adjournment, for experience proved that if a lie once gets a good start of the truth, it is difficult to overtake it."

div.head: SHOCKING DEATH OF A CHILD.
div.p: SHOCKING DEATH OF A CHILD.

A shocking occurrence took place at Warrington on Wednesday evening, when a little girl named May Whittaker, eight years of age, had her skull fractured by a grass-roller. The deceased was the daughter of Joseph Whittaker, a Cheshire Lines, Railway policeman, of 33, Leonard-st., off Battersby- latie. The child, according to the report that has been made to the Coroner, was with others playing on the cricket ground of the Cheshire Lines Committee, which is situate at Marsh House-lane. The roller used for the field, which weighs about 15cwts, was being pushed by some lads, and the deceased was knocked down. The roller caught her head, fracturing her skull. She only survived about five Minutes. Dr. Fox was summoned, and pronounced life extinct. Percy Whittaker, (13) a brother of the deceased, states that his sister was sitting on theroller with other children, when some boys pushed it. The others managed to get away, but deceased was knocked down. Ile helped to pull the troller back, and ran to help his sister. The other boys ran away. The de- ceased was carried home, but died just after arriving there. THE INQUEST: . .

_ Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquiry into the circumstances of the death at the Police Court Parade-room, yesterday afternpon. r Joseph Whittaker, 23 Leonard-st., a constable on the Cheshire Lines, deposed that the deceased was his daughter. She was eight years old. At about ten minutes to eight on the night in question the deceased was brought home by a person named George Harding. She had been badly injured about the head. Witness went to fetch Dr. Fox, and his daughter was dead when he returned. When she was brought home witness saw that her case was hopeless, but he thought it better to have a doctor. George Harding, 4, Leonard-st., a striker, gave evi- dence to the effect that at about 7.45 on Wednesday night he passed over the Cheshire Lines Cricket Club ground. He saw some children playing with the roller, and cautioned them. The roller weighed about 14 cwt. Witness's boy was among those playing, and he sent him' home. Soon afterwards witness heard a shout from the children, and .ran towards the roller. He found deceased on the ground. She was bleeding about the head. He picked her up, and, another man having tied a handker- chief round her head, witness carried her to the home of the parents. Witness did not often see children playing , with the Percy Whittaker, brother of the deceased, said that he, his sister, and other children, were playing with the roller, when some boys came up and pushed it. Deceased fell, and her head Was crushed by the roller. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the death was caused accidentally, and afterwards there was some conversation as to.what means could betaken to provide

against any similar accident occurring in the future. The Coroner pointed out that the children had no busi- ness to play with the roller, or to be on the around at all, as it was private property. The Secretary of the Cricket Club was present, and to him the jury suggested, through the Foreman, that the roller, when not in use, should be so protected that children could not play with it.
PENKETH. THE DROWNING CASE.

The inquest on the boy, G. Thompson, who was drowned in the canal at Penketh, was held at the Ferry Inn, by Mr. Husband, deputy-coroner, on Saturday. Mr. Thomas Garnett was the foreman of the jury. A verdict of "Found Drownea " was returned. •

div.head: TRAP ACCIDENT.
div.p: TRAP ACCIDENT.

At about half-past eight o'clock on Tuesday evening, as Mr. Henry Hughes, grocer, was return- ing home with Mr. Robert Fisher in his ( M.r. Fisher's) trap, it caught the curbstone near the Friends' School, and was overturned. Mr. Hughes was thrown into the road, and was severely shaken. He was conveyed home by Mr. and Mrs. Hampson and Mr. Joseph Carrington, of Great Sankey.

div.head: TRAP ACCIDENT..
div.p: A TRAP ACCIDENT..

On Monday an accident occurred in Penketh, by which Mr. H. Hughes was severely injured, Mr. Hughes, along with Mr. John Fisher and Mr J. Davies, were returning from Bold, and When opposite the Penketh School Nurseries, a party of cyclis's shot by, one of them passing right across the horse's head. The horse being a young colt, BMA and upset the party in the trap. Mr. Hughes was the only one to receive serious injury. He is confined to his bed, and it is likely to be some days before he gets over the effects of the accident.

div.head: DROWNING CASE.
div.p: THE DROWNING CASE.

An inquest Was held on Saturday, at, the Ferry Inn, on view of the body of James Henry Thomp- son (8), son of William Thompson, captain of the flat Amelia, who was drowned at about nine o'clock on Thursday last. Mr. W. T. Husband was the coroner. From the evidence of deceased's younger brother, a boy aged five years,..itAppeared that they were playing together on Thursday evening at about nine o'clock, on the canal bank near the bridge, and whilst attempting to reach a chip from the water deceased over-balanced himself and,fell in. Witness immediately called his father. -Wm. Thompson, the father, said he was called by his younger son, who told him that his brotlter, James Henry Thompson, had fallen into the canal. Witness came at once to the rescue, but it was too late, as no trace of the boy was to be seen. Grappling irons were procured, and the body was immediately recovered.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."
LYMI.

Tern Flotroays.—Hun—dred—s—of excursionists visited Lymm on Whit-Monday. For the benefit of the residents special trains were run to, Manchester, Belle Vue, Liver- pool, &c., which were well patronised. VOLUNTEER PRO/OM...NM—DRAM; the week, at Tatton Park, Lance-corporal H. Browning has been promoted to be corporal, and Lance-corporal Hugh Kirk to be corpo- ral. Both are members of the Lvmm corps. • , AN ACCIDENTAL DIP.—On Tuesday afternoon, when in the neighbourhood of Lymm Bridge, a navvy, who is said to have been drunk, accidentally tumbled into the canal. He was rescued from his predicament. THZ GAS MANAGER.—Mr. Graham, manager of the Gas Works for the Lymm Local Board, has been successful in getting the appointment of manager to the Gas Works at Hebden Bridge, in Yorkshire, from among 125 candi- dates. Mr. Graham has been in charge of the Lymm Gas Works for about four and a half years. FUNERAL.—The funeral of Percy E. Wynne (youngest son of Sergeant Wynne, of Lymm), who died after a brief illness on Friday, took place in the parish church- yard, on Monday. The Rev. R. Coward conducted tlke burial service. Several choice wreaths, including one from Miss Battersby, of Lymm Hall, were sent, POLICE CASES.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Tues- day morning, Thomas Ashley, a Ship Canal navvy, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Lymm the previous day. As this was defendant's first appearance, he was let Off with a fine of ss. including costs.—Joseph Price was summoned for a similar offence at the same time and place. A fine of 53. including costs was im- posed. Tns ANentwr ORDER OF DRUIDS The members of this order assembled at their lodge, on Monday, and paraded the village, calling at several residences en route. They afterwards partook of dinner at the Nag's Head Hotel. After the repast, which had been provided t‘y the landlord (Mr. Thomas Winstanley), votes of thanks were passed to the gentry of Lymm for their generosity to the lodge. The procession was headed through the village by the Lymm Church of England Brass Band, which after dinner played for about an hour on the lawn at the hotel for dancing. VOLUNTEERS IN CAMP.—The Lymm Company of the 3rd Volunteer Battalion Cheshire Regiment marched to Tatton Park on Saturday afternoon for their annual week's encampment. Captain T. A Jones was in coin- mend, and the other officers were Lieutenants Cookson and Groves. A halt was made at Broom Edge, where the Broom Edge and Heatley representatives joined the company. Camp was reached about six o'cleck. The men were subsequently inspected by Lieutenant-Colonel Fox. From the parade statement sheet it appears that the Lymm contingent represent •hree officers, seven ser geants. and 84 rank and file. ASSAULT BY NAVVIES.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Wednesday, Thomas McTighe, Mat Hannon, Peter Eden,l Patrick Macnamara, and James Cafferty were charged with assaulting Thomas Buxton, at Lymm, on the 26th May. The complainant and prisoners were navvies pm- ployed on the Ship Canal works, and lived near each other in the Rookery, at Lymm. On the day in question they quarrelled in a public-house. One of the men threatened to "lie in wait" for complainant. He sought police protection, and was taken home by two members of the local constabulary, but the prkoners followed him into his house and severely assaulted him.—The pris- oners were each fined 20s. and costs.

BANDS OF HOPE FESTIVAL. The second festival of the united Bands of Hope of 1 Lymm took place on Wednesday, in brilliant weather. All the denominations which have Bands of Hopel con- -1 necyted with their Sunday Schools took part in the cere- mony. The members of the various bands, with their 1 officers, began to assemble at the ancient Cross about 11.30 p.m., with their banners and regalia. The Parish Church band numbered about 200 members, Congrega- tional 260, Wesleyan 140, Baptists 80, and St. Peter's' (Oughtrington) 200, making, a grand total of 880 children. After the children had been mustered in proper order, they all sang three verses of the old hymn, "All people that on earth do dwell," and then marched up Eagle- brow to a field (kindly lent by Mrs. Grundy for the occasion) at the end of Madtman's-road. The following is the order of procession :—Two huntsmen, B. Stott and P. Ardern ; St. Mary's brass band ; St. Mary's Band of hope; Congregational Band of hope; St. Peter's Band of Hope, Oughtrington ; Baptist Band of Hope; Wesleyan Band of Hope ; Oughtrington drum and fife band ; two red cross knights on ponies, R. Heath- cote and T. Chorley • flower girls, H. Eaton, B A. Hind, E. Moston, M. Ardern, M. A. Wood, J. Daniels, M. Atkinson, E. Lord, A. Leigh, M. Percival, A. Barton, J. Warburton J. Percival, M. Lake, E Appleton, L. Win- stanley, M. Brooks, A. Odg,en, and M. Winstanley ; Japanese dancers, A. Knight, M. Hornby, H. Hinton, A. Kirk, J. Warburton, M. Moore, E. Wright, A. Moore, E. Joynson, P. Drinkwater, A. Rowlinson, A. Burrows, A. Johnson, A. Astley, and F. Ellison. Maypole dancers : E. Asprey, J. Ross, T. Worrall, L. Holt, A. Dixon, L. Warburton, L. Harrison, A. Branarck, 111. Diamond, M. Gibbon, T. Mills, E. Wright, E. Lake, E. Ardern, E. Sutton, A. Holt, E. Entwistle, J. Appleton, M. Drink- water, D. Daniels. Jack in the Green: J. Hussey. Scotchmen : 0. Elliott and J. Astbury. Irishmen: W. Diamond and J. Gibbon. Welsh girls : C. Marsland and D. Holt. American girls : fl. Ardern and A. Dandy. Japanese girls: C. Mairs, A. Rouse, N. Donald, A. ;Holt. S. Simpson, and E. Bradburn. Little Red Riding Hood: S. Cheetham. Grace Darling: C. Wrench. Foresters and Royal Beefeaters : E. Patterson, W. Winstanley, E. Caw- ley, and H. Holt. Crownand Sceptre Bearer: G. Gibbon and T. Heathcote. Band of Hope Queen (drawn in a carriage with two grey horses) : Miss Carrie Pickton, dressed in white cashmere and silk, with a train of purple velvet trimmed with swandown and lined with white silk. Her maids of honour, who followed in another carriage, were M. Elliott, L. Dalton, M. Mellor M. Warburton, E. Heaton, F. Brearley, S. Nixdn, and L. Ratcliffe. These were dresmed in white, muslin, with various coloured sashes and lace caps, in which were flowers to match the sashes. Next came the courtiers as follow :—G. Gibbon, G. Holt, H. Ratcliffe,' F. Copeland, and A. Astley, Cromwellian soldier on Pony, H. Gibbon. Queen's footgilards : G. Diamond, R. Littler, T. Holt, E. Mills, W. Hinton, A. Leigh, A. Cheetham, H. Jackson, T. Dutton, E. Mairs, E. Brad- burn, W. Haddon, B. Moston, W. Clare, D. Clare, W. Morris, D. Haddon, J. Wilkinson, J. Clare, J. Eaton, and J. Walker. Britannia and John Bull followed in a dray on which the insignia of F.Tigland's greatness was repre- sented, their names being A. Clare and J. Cadman. Next came four drays representing the four seasons, on which was a principal figure pour- traying the season, and surrounded by a number of boys appropriately dressed. The first was Spring (E. Thomason), Summei (J. Bowker), Autumn (S. Leah), Winter (C. Dawson.) The rear was brought up with a number of conveyances in which were the children who were too small to walk the round of the village, and two jockeys on ponies, named L. Jackson and J. Owen, com- pleted the procession. When the field was reached the bands were marched round the enclosure, and the queen walked in state, her train being borne by two pages in gorgeous apparel. She then took up her position on her throne, and her maids sat on the steps while her courtiers attended on her command. A Royal May-pole dance then took place, followed by a Japanese dance, and then

came the coronation, the crown being placed on the head of the queen by the bearer, G. Gibbon. After a move- ment of pages came a Scotch reel. The foot-guards were put through several evolutions by Mr. T. Warburton, who rode a charger. Another Royal May-pole dance and Japanese dance was fol- lowed by a tug of war in which a good deal of interest was taken, the soldiers winning an easy victory. A hymn was then sung and the order of procession was again formed, and the united Bands of Hope marched by way of Booth's-hill, Fligher-lane, Oughtrington-lane, Sandy-lane, and Rush-green to the Cross, where after the singing of another hymn they dispersed to their several schools, where a tea for each was provided at the expense of the committee. At 6.30 the elder members assembled at the Cross and returned to the field, where games of different kinds were indulged in until dark. Unstinted praise is due to the committee for the excellent arrangements made for the comfort uf the children, IMr. Nash, the M.C., and Mr. Harry Dorton, the hon. secretary, being indefatigable in the labours. The remainder of the committee were Messrs. J. Astley, T: Ardern, E. Brown, J. Blakemore, C. Midgley, H. Brown, E. Moston. H. Diamond, E. Clarke, and T. Griffiths. Mr. Dutton was the chairman and Mr. J. Dodds acted as the treasurer. No small share of praise is due to Miss Wheeler, Miss Moston, and Miss Hardman for the care they took in training the children to dance, their evolutions being exceedingly graceful. So highly pleased were the committee at the pains tak en by the drivers of the lurries that prizes were given. The first was awarded to Mrs. Cheeth.un and Mr. Allen, of Heatley ; the second to Mr. S. Heathcote ; and the third to Mr. E. Massey, of Cherry lane. In the evening the band of the Church of England Temperance Society played in the field for dancing, and Mr. Nash set off a number of balloons. Races were also extemporised for the scholars, and a most enjoyable day was brought to a close by the National Anthem. The tickets sold at the gate represent about 5,500 as having paid for admission.

div.head: IMPROVEMENT BILL.
div.p: THE IMPROVEMENT BILL.

With regard to the proposed extension of th e Warrington borough boundaries, the General Pur- poses Committee has passed the following resolu- tion, which '.ill be submitted to the Town Council at its meeting next Tuesday night:—" That on the advise of Counsel and the Parliamentary Agents, the township of Poulton be withdrawn from the proposed extension of the borough, and that notice thereof be given to Messrs. Hutchings.' The same Committee will recommend that the Town Clerk be authorized to insert clauses in , the Bill on behalf of the Cheshire County Council, providing for the adjustment of financial relations between the county and the Borough by the Local Govern- ment Board. The Town Clerk reports that, in ac- cordance with, the resolution of the General Par-

, poses Committee of the Bth instant, the Mayor and other representatives of the Corporation attended before the Lord Chairman of Committees, and went through his lordship's observations on the Bill. No material alteration was made in the Bill, and the interview with his lordship was considered very satisfactory.

div.head: RIVER MYSTERY AT RIXTON.
div.p: RIVER MYSTERY AT RIXTON.

On Thursday morning an inquest was held before the county coroner, Mr. Brighouse, at the Boat- house Inn, Rixton, near Warrington, relative to the death of a woman unknown, who was found dead on Sunda/ afternoon last floating in the Butchers- field Lock' of the Mersey and Irwe'll Canal at Rixton. Police-constable Mackae, stationed at Rixton, said he received information of the finding of the body. He had it taken out of the lock and removed to the Boathouse Ina. The body was very far advanced in decomposition, having apparently been in the water seven or eight weeks. Deceased was of dark complexion, and appeared to be thirty-five to forty years of age,. She was dressed in a dark dress, shawl, and,t?ther clothing. Nothing was found on the body to, lead to identity. The description had been sent to. the police in the surrounding districts, and the body had been photographed. The jury returned an open verdict.

div.head: WAIITtINGTOt TEMPERANCE FEDERATION AND THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.
div.p: WAIITtINGTOt TEMPERANCE FEDERA- TION AND THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.

A specially convened meeting of the Committee of the Warrington Temperance Federation was held on Wednesday evening, at the Horsemarket-street Cocoa Rooms, for the; purpose of considering the licensing proposals of;the Government. There was a very large attendance, and Mr. S. P. Stringer was voted to the chair. After considerable discussion it was resolved "That this meeting of the Warrington Temperance Federation earnestly protests against the proposal to allot money to County Councils for the purchase of licenses, believing that if such pro- posal become law it will create or lead to a vested interest in licenses." It was resolved that the fore- going resolution be forwarded to the member for the borough, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Lord Salisbury, Mr. Goschen, and Mr. Ritchie, It was also resolved to hold a further meeting in the Co-operative Hall, on Teealay next, for the purpose of recording an emphatic protest against the Government propo- sals. A large number of ministers and other gentle, men have promised to be present.

div.head: HOLIDAYS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE HOLIDAYS AT WARRINGTON.

Warrington people made holiday in earnest on Bank Holiday. The fine weather that was expe- rienced during the previous two or three days con- tinued, and a large number left home for the sea- side, and for Liverpool and Manchester, by the numerous excursion trains that were run by the Cheshire Lines Committee and the London and North-Western Railway. It is not the custom in , Warrington for the Sunday Schools to have proces- sions on Whit-monday, that being left to Walking Day, but some of them organised trips to country places within a moderate distance. Several hun- dred children, who live at the Ship Canal villages ' in the neighbourhood, had a treat provided at Thel- wall. During the day the streets were quiet, all the places of business being closed, and a great portion of the population being out of town, but in the evening they had a brisker appearance. At- tractions for the evening were provided at the Theatre Royal, the Public Hall, and the Sankey-st. circus, all of which places of amusement were freely patronised. In the afternoon there were numerous visitors to Bank Park gardens, which just now are looking at their best. The weather was fine all day, and, locally speaking, the holiday was an unusually enjoyable one. The traffic on both lines of railway running through Warrington as exceptionally heavy, and the officials had their exertions greatly taxed in regulating it.

div.head: RECENT BURGLARY AT WARRINGTON. COMMITTAL OF THE PRISONERS._
div.p: THE RECENT BURGLARY AT WARRINGTON. COMMITTAL OF THE PRISONERS._

At the Birkenhead Police Court yesterday, before Mr. Preston, stipendiary magistrate, two young men named George Bennett and Frederick Foster were charged on remand with breaking and entering the lock-up shop of Francis Noel Cumine (trading as Albert Cole and Co.), 482, New Chester-road, and with stealing a quantity of biscuits, cheese, and other articles ; also breaking and entering the lock-up shop of Messrs. Sielton Brothers. Horse Market-street, Warrington, and stealing a number of pocket knives, pistols, razors, boots, and other articles, their property. They were further charged with being in unlawful possession of dangerous weapons. Mr. R. B. Moore prosecuted, and stated that on the mornin., of the 23d inst. Police-constable Moore heard a noise in Mr. Cumine's shop. He whistled for assistance, and several officers came up. They entered the premises and found both prisoners, who had each a loaded revolver in his possession. The revolvers were indentified as having been stolen with other property from the shop of Mr. Skelton, at Warrington, on the previous Tuesday night or Wednesday morning. The revolvers were not loaded on the Tuesday evening when the shop was closed, but the prisoners had also stolen a number of cartridges. He merely stated this to show the dangerous character of the prisoners, because if they did not mean mischief they would not have loaded the revolvers. Evidence I was then given by Police Constables Moore and Raven- ' hill and Inspector Waugh as to the prisoners, whose boots were found in the backyard, the prisoners having only their stockings on. When Bennett opened the door he said to the officer, " It is a clean cop, old man," and put his hand into his breast pocket, from which he I took a revolver, remarking "I think I had bctter quieten one or two of you." Inspector Waugh seized i hold of the revolver and wrenched t from the prisoner Bennett, who immediately told his companion to give up his revolver, .which did. Both prisoners were then locked up, and in their possessioa was found the property stolen at Warrington and several pairs of socks. Mr. Cumine's shop had been ramsaclied, the drawers being forced open, and the prisoners had in- dulged irk biscuits and gorgonzola cheese, jellies, choco- late creams, and other delicacies. Evidence of the War- rington robbery having been given, Bridewell-keeper Parker stated that after being remanded he visited the prisoner Bennett in his cell, and he told hitn where the remainder of the stolen property could he fotpci buried under a tree at the old lane. New F.rriz. Witness went to the place indicated, and found the propertv. Prisoners were committed for trial.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
A meeting of this Council will be held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening.
THE PAVING OF BIZIC _YARDS,.

The Paving and Sewerage Committee will recommend that the sub-committee, with Councillors Fleming and Flood be requested to report to the Cumtnitte- with reference to the paving of public back yards within the borough.

div.head: ON THE ALERT.
div.p: ON THE ALERT.

The General Purposes Committee recommend that the Town Clerk instruct the London Agents to watch the fol- lowing Bills, on behalf of the Cotporation, and, if it should be found necessary, that petitions be prepared and presented against the Bills, namely :—The London and North-Western Railway Bill ; the Manchester Ship Canal (various powers) Bill.
THE NEW COUNCILLOR.
Councillor Beaman has been appointed a member of the School Attendance Committee.
THE CORPORATION AND THE INFIR-
MARY EXTENSION.

It will be remembered that at a meeting of the Warrington Town Council held two or three months ago, a unanimous opinion was expressed in favour of granting a piece of land for the site of the pro- posed extension of the local infirmary. Since then some negotiations have taken place between the representatives of the Infirmary and the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee, and some difficul- ties have arisen as to the exact site to be granted. The Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee in their minutes which are to be submitted to the Town Council, on Tuesday evening, state that Alderman Davies, Major Litton; and Mr. Wilson, attended on behalf of the In- firmary Committee, and stated their views with respect to the land required for the extension of the Infirmary. After considering the suggestions of the Infirmary Com- mittee, and after visiting the site, it was resolved, "that thg Committee regret that they cannot see their way to agree to the plan preparedby the Infirmary Committee." The Borough Surveyor was instructed to prepare plans of two alternative schemes, and to submit the same to the Infirmary Committee for their consideration. At a meeting of the Board of Management of the Infirmary held yesterday Mr. W. Owen attended and re ported the refusal of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths - Committee to grant the land asked for by the Board. The Committee had, however, forwarded plans of two alternative plots for consideration. It was resolved that the chairman should arrange for a deputation from the Buildings and Workingmen's Committees to have an interview with the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Com- mittee with a view to arranging matters.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THIIRSDA.T.—Before his Honour Judge FfoulkeS. THE CAUSE LIST comprised 2 default summonses, 12 adjourned plaints. 208 original plaints, and 43 judgment summonses. A HORSE TRANSACTION.—Joseph Young, labourer, Ship ICanal Huts, Acton Grange, brought an action against Mary Mulholland, second-hand furniture dealer, Mersey. at., Warrington, for damages for breach of warranty, Mr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, Mr. P. Davies for the defendant, and a jury was empanelled to hear the case.—Mr. Browne said that the defendant was a second- . hand furniture dealer, and, being separated from her husband, carried on business on her own account. On the 27th of last April, which was a Sunday, an exchange took place between Mrs. Mulholland and the plaintiff, of a horse, and of a pony, cart, and gears. Plaintiff had at that time a small pony, and wanted a larger one to carry passengers from Warrington to Acton Grange. The whole transaction took place on a Sunday. The parties drove to Winwick Hall ley, where defendant had a horse, which was pointed out to plaintiff as being the one that she was willing to exchange. Ultimately it was arranged that plaintiff should have the horse, and that in return the defendant should receive his pony, cart, and gears, with £1 to boot. Mrs. Mulholland, Mr. Browne con- tended, guarranteed the horse to be sound, and it was afterwards found, upon examination by a veterinary surgeon, that it was not sound, and was, in fact, only worth about 10s. It would have been cruelty on the part of the plaintiff to work it. Evidence was then called in support of the case for the plaintiff, the witnesses being cross-examined at length by Mr. Davies as to what took place when the exchange was agreed upon.—Mr. J. F. Dixon, V.S. was called for the plaintiff, and said that when called to see the horse he found it suffering from lameness in the off-hind leg, which was ulcerated and enlarged. It would have been cruelty to work the animal in its then condition, but with constant treatment by a veterinary surgeon the ulcer- ation might be cured in three months. The horse in that case would be worth £2o.—The defendant was then called, and denied having told the plaintiff that the horse was sound.—Mr. Davies contended that no warranty had been given by the defendant as to the soundness of the horse.—His Honour then summed up the case at length, after which the jury retired. On their return, after a short absence, the Foreman intimated that they were not able to agree.—Bis Honour: Are there three on one side and two on the other P—The Foreman said that one of the jurymen was neutral. He did not think they could agree.—His Honour then discharged the jury. A MUSICIAN'S CLAIM.—Anne Sutton, of Market-street, Warrington, sued John Bolsworth, of Winwick-street, Warrington, for two guineas, being the amount agreed to be paid by him for playing the pianoforte for dam-. ing. Mr. Longton appeared for the plaintiff, and said that the defendant arranged with the plaintiff that she should play for him for dancing at his it.CO of business for one quarter, and he was to pay her the sum of two guineas. No fault had been found with her playing, the only defence appareetr being that she did not turn up one night when she ought Ito have done. Mr. A. Browne for the defence said that the defendant engaged the plaintiff believing she Was a. competent person to play the piano. lie; howeber, dis- covered that she was incompetent. She played the wrong music for dances and the pupils began to com- plain. It was also alleged that the plaintiff was not punctual in her attendances, and on one occasion did not turn up at all, in consequence of which the whole of the pupils bad to go away, the class being almost spoiled. Mr. Browne further submitted that if anybody was responsible it was Mrs. Bolsworth, who kept a con- fectioners shop apart from"her husband, and also carried on the dancing class on her own account. Witnesses having been called by Mr. Brown, and Mr. Longton hav- ing replied, a verdict was given for the defendant.

div.head: SIR It. PEEL VICTIMIZED.
div.p: SIR It. PEEL VICTIMIZED.

The American newspapers publish long accounts of the neat manner in which Sir Robert Peel and Mr. Clifford Talbot were victimized by an American s windier whom they met on board the Aurania, which arrived at New I York on Sunday. The swindler gave the name of Russell, and said he was one of the principal detectives of the New York Police Department. His appearance was pre- possessing, and he was a good talker, and won the friend- ship of the Englishmen by his tales of romantic adven- tures as a detective. He said he was returning home from Germany, where he had been to deliver to the Berlin authorities a notorious forger, who had been arrested in America, and that he would receive upon landing at New York £BOO from the German Consul as a reward for the service. He placed himself at the disposal of the strangers, and offered to show them about the city. The gentlemen completely deceived by the manner of the man, gladly accepted his services, and upon landing they all went to the Hoffman House, and then to secure rooms. Russell piloted them about the city, living in great style at the expense of the Englishmen. The latter were very de- sirous of being presented to Byrnes, the chief of the de- tective department, but their new friend was able to invent excuses which satisfied them. Meanwhile he re- ceived many presents from the liberal Englishmen. Sir Robert Peel; it is said, presented him with a pearl and diamond scarf-pin, valued at £l6O, and Mr. Talbot gave him a handsome chain-bracelet as a souvenir of their ac- quaintanceship. Mr. Talbot went on Tuesday night to Chicago, but before leaving dined with Sir Robert and Russell at Delmonico's. Unfortunately for Russell, two detectives paid a visit to the same estab- lishment while the dinner was in progress, and at once recognised in him a man of whom they had been in search. They waited patiently till the dinner was finished, when Russell came out with the Englishmen and called for a cab for Mr. Talbot. The detective then arrested Mtn en a charge of obtaining from a widow, whom he had promised to marry two years ago, a con- siderable sum of money, with which he fled to Europe, and also with stealing 200 dollars from an insurance company while a clerk. The plisoner's real name is McDermott. He was formerly a cabdriver, and has a long record as a swindler. Sir Robert Peel was dumb- founded by the revelation. In addition to giving Russel/ valuable presents, he had entrusted him with four five- pound Bank of England notes to be exchanged into American money, and an order for his luggage. Both were returned to him after the arrest, with Mr. Talbot's bracelet.

div.head: BRAylt RESCUE BY A LABoITRER AT STOCKTON
div.p: BRAylt RESCUE BY A LABoITRER AT STOCKTON

HEATH At about half-past three o'clock on Sunday after- noon a child, three years old, son of James Percival, carter, Stockton Heath, was playing on the canal side near the bridge there, when it slipped into the water. An older child who was with it at the time gave the alarm, when Daniel Hamblett, a labourer employed at Stockton Quay, jumped into the water and rescued the little one a it was going down for the second time. He was himolf exhausted when got out of the water, as he had run a distance of 200 yards before getting to the canal side. When the child was brought out of the water it was in an unconscious condition, hut the usual treatment in the ease of the apparently drowned CV:IS adopted by Sir. E. DaDow and others, who had been attracted to the sot, and the child was soon brought round.

div.head: Too MANY SCHOOLS AND Too LITTLE SCHOOLING.
div.p: Too MANY SCHOOLS AND Too LITTLE SCHOOLING.

-- At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday morn- ng, a etse was heard in which James Amiss, forgeman, Tanners's-lane, was charged with having neglected to regularly send his son to school. Mr. G. Riley who pro- secuted on behalf of the School Attendance Committee, said that the case was the most flagrant one he had known. The lad had attended nearly all the schools in the town at different times, but at none of them was his attendance regular. Among the schools he had been to were mentioned Wycliffe, the National, Heath Side, Roman Catholic, Hamilton-st., Orford-lane, and St. Anne's. They wanted a school especially building for the lad, Mr. Riley added. It was the most troublesome case he had ever heard of. The magistrates at the request of Mr. Riley, sent the boy, an intelligent looking one, to the Ship Clio. Mrs. Amiss said that the decision was very hard, but the magistrates replied that she her- self was greatly to blame in the matter.

div.head: WIFE A&SAULT.
div.p: WIFE A&SAULT.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, Michael Kenney was charged with having assaulted his wife on the 29th inst. Mrs. Kenney said she had been mar- ried to the prisoner eighteen months, and he had several times struck her. He had now smashed all the furni- ture. Constable Frank Jones deposed to apprehending the prisoner at his home. The officer said that the pic- tures were smashed to pieces, and the floor was covered with glass There was scarcely a piece of furniture un- broken in the house.—Alderman Harrison (to complain- ant) : How came you to marry such a scoundrel ? Complainant: I don't know, sir.—Alderman Harrison: I think you must have teen bereft of your senses.—Pri- soner said that he was sorry.—Alderman Harrison :Don't insult one's commonsense by saying that. You are not worthy the name of a man.—The Bench ordered prisoner to go to jail for a month, and granted the wife a judicial seperation order, uuder which the husband will have to pay her ss. a week. A PUBLIC-HOUSE " LARK."

James Rowson, a young man, was charged at War- rington Police Court, on Saturday with having assaulted Joseph Wilshaw,who is better known among his inti- mates as" Black Joe." Mr. P. Davies defended. Com- plainant's evidence was to the effect that when in the Red Lion Inn. Rowson put somebody's cap up a chimney and then blacked complainant's face with soot. After they left the house Rowson struck Wilshaw disfiguring his face. The story for the defence was altogether differ- ent, and it was supported by two or three witnesses. It was admitted that some" larking "had been going on in which " Black Joe's" face had been made blacker. In consequence of this Wilshaw harboured resentment,went home and got some cayenne pepper or snuff which he threw into Rowsen's face as the latter left the public- house. After doing this Wilshaw, it was said, ran away and falling down bruised his face. He was not struck by anyone. The case was dismissed, the bench remark- ing that such a charge should not have been brought by complainant without better evidence. A BANK-HOLIDAY TRIPPER'S ADVENTURE.

A respectably dressed middle-aged woman, who gave the name of Margaret Barry, and who hails from Liver- pool, was before the Warrington magistrates on Tuesday morning, on two charges. One was of having been drunk and disorderly at the Central station, on the night before, and the other was of having assaulted Benjamin Higson, fcreman pointer, at the same time and place. Higson said that at about 945 on Monday night he was on duty at the Central Station, when a train from Manchester came in. Prisoner was in a com- partment fighting with some other passengers. She was taken from the compartment, and when on the platform conducted herself as though she were mad. It took six or seven persons to hold her down and she struck wit- ness across the face. Afterwards she hit him on the head with a basket. When taken into custody by the police it was stated, she threw herself down again, and had to be taken to the Bridewell in a hand-cart.—Mr. R. Garnett: The assumption is that if she was drunk at Warrington she would be drunk when she got into the train at Manchester.—Mr. Hunt: It is hard to tell. People sometimes carry bottles.—The magistrates fined prisoner ss. and costs for each offence.

ALLEGED ASSAULT AT STOCKTON HEATll.—Thomas Pittem was summoned for having on the 21st May, at Stockton Heath, assaulted Win. Bostock; builder, and a man named Edward Jones.—Mr. Arthur Browne defend- ed.—From the evidence it appeared that on the day in question a dispute arose between Mr. Bostock and the defendant with reference to the removal of nightsoil from houses belonging to them, and situated near each other at Stockton Heath. The result was the alleged as- sault. Several witnesses were called, one of whom in answer to Mr. Browne, said he thought "one as bad as another." He alluded to Pittem and Jones.—Mr. Browne, for the defence, contended that the complainant Bostock had no right to wheel a wheel-barrow over Pittem's premises, nor tip refuse at his back door. With refer- ence to the assault upon Bostock, he said that Pittem simply pushed him off the premises. No more force was used than was necessary.—Benjamin Gash gave corroborative evidence, and said Bostock was not pushed against the wall.—The Bench dismissed the case.

WARRINGTON v. NEW BRIGHTON.—After an absence of a few seasons New Brighton re-appeared on the Warring- ton ground on Saturday. Through the visitors' late arrival it was 2.55 p.m. before Woodward (pro.) and Hull commenced batting, the former getting Jolley's first ball away for four. The score was carried to 22, when Hull was beaten. J. D. Walsh opened with a four, but with the score at 35 J. J. Crosfield took the ball from Smith, and five runs later S. M. Crosfield displaced Jolley ; the latter chang) woiking at once; two wickets fell in his first over. England's was only a short stay, and, with 51 for four wickets, Percival (pro.) joined Woodward. Both men scored freely, and brought on several changes of bowling, but it was not untikthe score had reached 123 that Whitley broke through Per- cival's defence. In his. 35 were four fours. Edwards was bowled first ball, and when Duerden got with the pro. another stand was made, Duerden being the first to go with 27 to his credit, the result of good cricket-7 for 178. Six runs later Woodward was snapped by Arm- strong for an invaluable N. He had been at the wicket about three hours, and hit 13 fours. When he had scored nine he almost lost his wicket through a splendid piece of fielding between Podmore and Smith. Two difficult chances were given in the slips when he had made 54, his last 40 being without blemish.—Warrington, with about an hour to bat, started with S. M. and J. J. Cros- field, the former being given lbw before he had scored— one for five. Smith and Crosfield played lively cricket, the former retiring at 38, his fourteen made up of three fours and two singles. Whitby and Crosfield from this point treated every bowler alike, and notwithstanding repeated changes were both not out at the call of time, having carried the score from 38 to 119. Mr. Crosfield has seldom shown better form ; his 50 was scored with- out giving a chance. Whitby should certainly have been easily caught by Goodacre when he had made 35. Included in his 51 were eight fours. Crosfield hit six fours.—The following is the full score NEW BRIGHTON. ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

After the weak display of the Surrey men on Friday • afternoon, the Australians were only left with /9 runs to get on Saturday to win, and no =in having fallen during the night the task was a very easy one. About an hour and twenty minutes' cricket proved sufficient to finish off the match, and thanks to some capital batting by Trott and Murdoch, the necessary number of runs were hit off for the loss of only two wickets. Victory. thus rested with the Colonial team by the substantial majority of eight wickets. They showed better form than the Surrey men at all points of the game. The bowling honours belong to Sharpe, who took five wickets for 62 runs, and Lyons, who captured eight wickets for 84 runs. It may be mentioned that so far Murdoch's average is 31.2 runs for seven completed innings. He is at the head of the Australian's list, of course, Lyons and Turner coming next.

In the cricket field on Saturday the Australians beat Surrey by bight wickets, Gloucestershire were defeated by Kent, and Oxford University went down before the Gentlemen of England. At Manchester, on Tuesday, Lancashire gained a decisive victory over Kent 'by an innings and 68 runs. The Australians were defeated by Yorkshire, at Sheffield, by seven wickets. At Lord's, Somersetshire beat Middlesex by 78 runs; while Derby- shire defeated F.s.c.Px, at Leyton. by eight runs.

Dr. W. G. Grace contributes a capital article on cricket to the June number of the "English Illustrated Magazine." A. G. Steel, lit describes as " One of the best all-round cricketers it has been my lot to meet dur- ing my long career." W. W. Read is thus spoken of: "As good a batsman as we have at the present time ;" and Shrewsbury as the "finest professional batsman." Lohmann is "one of the best all-round cricketers," his bowling on a sticky wicket being" simply unplavable." Briggs is declared to be " one of the most difficult bowl- ers of the day," and the" best cover point," which we fully endorse.

The cricket match between Notts and Surrey ended on Wednesday, in a win for the former, by 108 runs. Sussex at Brighton, after declaring their second inning d closed with seven wickets down and Quaife not out 158, inflic- ted a severe defeat upon Gloucestershire; and Warwick- shire beat Leicestershire by five wickets.

MISCELLANEOUS. An electric lamp for cycles is stated to have been per- fected, which will give a continuous light for 15 hours. Its weight is Albs., but its price is not stated. That of a primary battery to charge it is es., and the cost will not be more than id, an hour. If this is true, and the article put on the market at a reasonable figure, oil lamps will soon become a drug.
WHITSIINAIDE FESTIVITIES AT ST.

_ HELENS. The popular Whitsuntide holiday has bad a very general observance at St. Helens. As in former years all places of business and the various chemical and glassworks in the district were closed on Mon- day, and happily for the comfort of the many thousands of excursionists who left the town and the still greater number of pleasure seekers who stayed at home the weather was of the most favour- able character. From an early hour in the morning the scene at the railway statiox was of 'an animated character. The passenger traffic was greatly in excess of that of any former year, and about 10,000 left by the special and ordinary trains which were run to Southport, Blackpool, Liverpool, Manchester, North Wales, and other plices of interest. Of this total about 2,550 booked to Liverpool; 2,800 to Southport ; 2.000 to Blackpool ; 350 to Belle Vue ; 300 to North Wales; 50 to Winder- mere; and about 2,250 were taken to other centres. The railway company's servants under Mr. Moss, station- master, and Mr. James, chief clerk, performed their duties with remarkable energy, and the trains were des- patched with considerable punctuality. There were not many public attractions in St. Helens. In the afternoon several school treats took place, and these were very largely attended by the children. Reports of the various Whitsuntide celebrations are appended.

div.head: CATHOLIC CHURCHES.
div.p: CATHOLIC CHURCHES.

As Whit Sunday is one of the most important of the festivals celebrated by the Catholic Church, there was Solemn High Mass in all the Catholic churches on Sunday and efforts were made to celebrate the festival in a be- coming manner. It being also the last Sunday of May there were processions in honour of the Blessed Virgin. At Lowe House Church Gdunod's " Messe Solennelle " was rendered by the choir ma pleasing style,the soloists being Mrs. 0. M. Barton and Mrs. V. Barton (sopranos', Mrs. Williams (contralto), Messrs. G. Barton, jun., and B. S. Henty (tenors), and Mr. F. Dennett (bass), accompanied by the organist, Mr. 0. M. Barton. The Rev. Father Kenny preached at the morning service, while the Rev. Father Brown was the preacher at the evening service. At Holy Cross Church the Rev. Father Gradwell was the celebrant at Solemn High Mass, and he was assisted by two German father. The choir gave an exceptionally fine rendering of Beethoven's Mass in C,theprincipal soloists being Miss H. Swift (soprano), Miss Sanderson (con- tralto)l Mr. Barr (tenor), and Mr. John Sephton (bass). Mr. J. Unsvrorth presided at the organ. At the Sacred Heart Church the Rev. Father Dobson sang the Missa Cantata, and the Very Rev. Dean Walmsley preached an instructive sermon from the words "And they were filled with the Holy Ghost." The choir sang the "Kyrie" and " Gloria " from Mozart's Seventh Mass, and the " Benedictus," " Santus," and " Agnus Del," ofrom Weber's Mass in G, the whole of which were very satis- factorily rendered, the soloists being Miss J. Oldham (soprano), Misses Wilcock and Middlehurst (contralto), Mr. A. G. Coope (tenor), and Mr. T. McHale (bass). The baton was ably wielded by Mr. A. E. Coope.
THE RAILWAY EXCURSIONS.

- The railway excursions on Monday morning attracted an immense crowd to the railway station. Under the auspices of the St. Helens Liberal Association there were special trains to Blackpool and to Southport, about 900 people Journeying, to the " Brighton of the North"' and 800 proceeding to Southport. The arrangements for the trips were carried Out, principally by Councillor John Forster and Councillor H. Martin. About 750 passengers were also conveyed to Blackpool in connection with the St. Thomas's Church excursion; while the Kirkland-st. Primitive Methodists had a cheap train to Southport and took over 850 persons, including the band and a number of the members of the Salvation Army: The Sutton-road Wesleyan Sunday School had an excursion to Rhyl and Llandudno, and about 250 passengers were conveyed to North Wales. In connection with the Sutton Conserva- tive Club, about 1,000 trippers left for Blackpool. In addition to these: guaranteed excursions the railway company issued cheap return tickets to many centres of interest and all the trains were well filled.
SCHOOL TREATS.

There were several school treats on Whit-Monday afternoon. . One of the most successful was the joint demonstration in connection with the Parish Church School, and the York-street Mission School. The two sections amalgamated at the Parish Church schools, and the monstre ploceeien, numbering nearly 2,000 child- ren, was headed by the York-Street brass band. Among those present were the Rev. Canon Eyre, M.A., Rev. E. V. Everard, Rev. H. A. Arnold, and other gentlemen and ladies. who showed great interest in attending to the wants and comfort of the little ones. The processionists marched to Littler's field, at Denton's Green, where the

ST. HELENS CHARITY ORGANISATION SOCIETY. The annual meeting of the subscribers to the St. Helens Charity Organisation Society was held at the Town Hall, on Friday afternoon. The Mayor (Alderman C. J. Bishop) presided, and there were

also present CouncilkiH Martin, Rev. W. Flaherty, Rev. G. Lakeman, Rev. W. W. Spencer, Rev. C. F. Aked, Messrs. B. A Dromgoole, A. J. Speeden (hon. treasurer) and F. Dromgoole t (hon. sec.) The Mayor remarked that they had met td hold the third annual meeting, and he called upon the secretary to submit the annual report.—A summary of the report, printed copies of which had been distributed, has previously appeared in our columns, and on the motion of Mr. Dromgoole, seconded by Mr. Martin,the report was formally adopted. " —Councillor H. Martin moved the re-appointment of Mr. A. J. Speeden as hon. treasurer, and of Mr. F. Dromgoole as hon. sec. Rev. W. W. Spencer seconded the motion, which was adopted.—The Mayor stated that the next business was the election of twelve members to serve on the Executive, and the following were appointed: Alder- men T. Cook, D. Gamble, Messrs. C. J. Critchley, C. Cul- shaw, A. Dennett, B. A. Dromgoole, J. C. Eccles, James Marsh, A. H. Michell, W. W. Pilkington, J. Saxon, and H. Martin.—The Mayor afterwards moved a vote of thanks to the Executive Committee for their services during the past year, and the Rev. G. Laketnan seconded the motion which was adopted.—The Mayor said there was a question for consideration in reference to the appointment of female visitors.—Mr. Dromgoole said that such appointments had been suggested with the view of seeing that relief in kind got to its proper channel. Some correspondence had taken place in reference to the subject, and he thought it would be best to refer the matter to the Executive.—This course was adopted.— The Secretary stated that at a meeting of the Executive Committee a discussion had taken place as to whether the society might not deal with the question of cruelty to children, and it was thought they might join the national society with that object. He had written to the society in question, and he had received a letter that morning stating that experience had taught them that their work could not be satisfactorily carried out in connection with any other existing institution at present. They regretted it was so, but they had tried it and it proved efailure.— The Mayor thought the matter could be left in the hands of the Executive Committee.—The Rev. C. F. Aked said the charity organisation might very well take up the question of cruelty to children, as they had plenty of opportunity for doing so.—The Mayor supposed they k could do practically the same work as the national society whether or not they were affiliated to it.—Mr. B. A. Dromgoole suggested that the Executive Committee should be instructed to consider the matter, and moved a resolution to that effect. The Rev. W. W. Spencer

seconded, and the motion was adopted.—The Mayor moved a vote of thanks to the secretary and treasurer, and the Rev. W. Flaherty seconded. On the motion of the Rev. W. W. Spencer, a similar compliment was paid to the Mayor, and the meeting terminated.

ST. , HELENS VOLUNTEERS IN CAMP. A very large crowd assembled in the 4icinity of the railway station, on Friday night, to witness tlie departure of the 2nd Volfinteer Battalion of Me South Lancashire Regiment for a week's encamp- ment near Layton Hall, Blackpool. The men mustered at their headquarters. the Volunteer Hall, where about 400 rank and file assembled. Headed by the baud of the battalion, under Band-Master Hall, they marched to the station, and left for their encampment, by special train, shortly before half-past seven. Colonel W. W. Pilkington was in command, and the other officers present were Colonels R. Pilkington and White, Majors Cook and Mc Fear; Captain and Ad- jutant Jacob, Captains Wolfenden, Dickinson, Shaw, Hadley, Lewis, D. Gamble, and Gossage ; Lieutenants Thompson, McTear, Hopgood, White, Plews, Thomas, and Webb, and Surgeon F. J. Knowles. A fatigue party under Quarter-Master Balshaw had left St. Helens for the site of the camp on the previous Tuesday, in order to make the usual preparations. About 100 men who were unable to accompany their comrades on the Friday night joined the battalion on Saturday. The battalion arrived at Blackpool shortly after nine o'clock on Friday night, and they were at once formed into marching order and proceeded to the camping ground. Here there were twenty-three tents in the officers' lines' besides a large marquee, used as the dining room and lounge. In the non-commissioned officers' and privates' lines there were sixty-eight tents, besides the orderly and stores tents, the sergeants' mess tent, and cooking kitchens, canteen, &c. The men were told off to their tents by Quarter- master Balshaw and Quartermaster-Sergeant Wallace. On Saturday morning the real work of the camp com- menced. On Sunday morning divine service was held in camp, Captain and Adjutant Jacobs reading the les- sons aind prayers. The band, under the conductorship of Bandmaster F. Hall, contributed the musical part of the service. On Monday morning, at the commanding officers' parade, Lieutenant-Colonel Pilkington practised the battalion in the new " attack" movement. After- wards a very pleasing ceremony took place, when the certificates' were presented by Lieutenant-Colonel R. Pilkington to the members of the St. John Ambulance class, formed in connection with the corps, who had been ' successful in the recent examination. The members pre- sented Surgeon Major Knowles, who had delivered the lectures of the class, with a splendid meerschaum pipef and Sergeant-Major Tyson was the recipient of a hand- • some cruet stand. The camp broke up on Wednesday, and the men returned to St. Helens.

afternoon was pleasantly spent in variousgames. Sports and amusements of various kinds were provided, and the children were supplied with tea, scones,sandwiches, &c. The members of the Band of Hope Society connected with Brook-st. Congregational Schools, joined by the members.of Gerard's Bridge and Knowsley-rd., had their annual gala on Monday afternoon. The muster was made at the various schools, and having united in pro- cessional order at Brook-st., they proceeded to Sephton's field, at Flaresfinch. They procession consisted of over 1.000 persons, was headed by the Cave Brown Protestant Brass Band, and was in charge of the Rev. R. J. Ward, Rev. W. Arthur,' and others. During the afternoon tea was served out.—rhe members of the Nutgrove Wesleyan Sunday School Band of Hope to the number of 450, left the school, headed by the Nut- grove Temperance Brass band, and proceeded to a field adjoining Elton Head Farm, kindly lent for the occasion by Mrs. John Lowe. After they, had partaken of buns and milk, a variety of sports were indulged in by the young people.—The Peasley Cress Congregational and of Hope members, marched to a field at Marshall's Cross, where they had sports conducted by the Rev. W., Parry and the teachers.

div.head: SHIP CANAL MYSTERY.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL MYSTERY.

PRISONER BEFORE THE LEIGH MAGISTRATES. Contrary to expectation. Mr. Superintendent Weir brought the prisoner Vaughan to Leigh on Saturday afternoon, and the same evening he was taken before Dr. Evans and charged with wilfully killing Thomas Elliman, an engineer employed on the Ship Canal works at Rixton; On the 27th April. Mr. Weir gave evidence to the effect that he received prisoner into custody from the Ross police. On arriving at Leigh he charged Vaughan with wilfully killing Elliman. In reply he said "No. not wilful, it was an accident; he did it himself. We were neither of us doing anything. I had just washed my boilers out,and I was waiting for him to get the water away before I started to pump. He called toe and told me to bring that thing up. I took my re- volver out of this coat pocket (meaning the one he was wearing), and put it in my blue coat pocket. I showed it to deceased. He was doing something with it. I turned my back and heard him call out almost immedi- ately afterwards, Oh, I have shot myself.' I turned round again and saw he was going to fall. I caught him and he died with his head on my arm. I was frightened. The man that he lodged with came down and told me to go and fetch the walking ganger. I went away. I thought all the barrels (meaning chambers) were dis- charged." The prisoner was remanded until next morning. On Monday morning Vaughan was again brought before the magistrates at Leigh. There were on the bench Messrs. F. W. D. Bouth (chairman), C. Wright, M.P., R. Fletcher, A. Burrows 0. P. Lancashire, and W. Tunnicliffe.—Simerintenderit Weir gave evidence. He said that en the 27th April, or the morning of the 28th, he received information of an affair which took place on the Manchester Ship Canal Werka at Rixton. He visited the place, and found on inquiry there that a , person named Thomas Elliman, an engineer, had been shot dead in the cutting. An inquest was opened and adjourned, and there had been a still further adjourn- inept until the 3rd of next month. Thia man, Vaughan, was mentioned as having been seen at the place when the shot was heard; and on Friday last witness received him into custody at Ross 4 Here- fordshire. He brought him to Leigh on Saturday, and on the way cautioned him, and then Old him he was charged with wilfully murdering Thomas Elliman by shooting him with a pistol and bullet in the cutting of the Manchester Ship Canal on Sunday, the 27th April. He replied: " Wilful I No, it was not wilful! it was an accident. I did not shoot him; he shot himself. I had nothing to shoot him for. I will tell you all about it." He then made a long statement, which it was not necessary to go into unless the Bench desired. Witness asked the Bench to remand prisoner to Warrington next day. The Chairman: What is the prisoner's name P—Mr. Weir : He has been known as Frederick Edwin Vaughan. He says now his name is Edwin William Vaughan.—The Chairman said the Iprisoner would be remanded to the Sessions at Warring- ton, and he was then removed. PRISONER BROUGHT UP AT WARRINGTON. On Tuescjay morning prisoner was"brought up at the Warrington Occasional Court, before Captain T. E. Withington, a county magistrate when he was again 'charged with the murder of Elliman. Superintendent Weir stated that on Sunday, the 27th April. a man ,named Thomas Elliman was found lying dead in a cut- ting of the Madchester Ship Canal at Rixton. From inquiries which witness had made, he believed that the prisoner was the last person seen in the company of the deceased. Inquiries were made for Vaugha.6, and it was found that he had disappeared from the district. Witness had the usual intimation given to all the police officers in the country. Prisoner, he believed, surren- dered himself to the police at a place near to Ross, in Herefordshire, on the previous Friday morning. On the same day witness received him into custody from the police there, and took him to Leigh On the way he charged him with the offence, and prisoner gave a reply similar to the one the superintendent detailed when the case was before the Leigh magistrates: He asked for a remand until the 4th of next month.—Captain Within g- ton : Have you any reason why you should not he re- manded.—Prisoner : No, Sir.—Prisoner was then for- mally remanded. - STATEMENT BY THE PRISONER'S FATHER. Thomas Brown Vaughan, farmer at Linton, near Ross, the father of the prisoner, has made a statement to the effect that the first the iamily heard of the affair was from a son-in-law, who lives near Wigan. He (the father) advertised telling his son to give himself up, but heare nothing of him. He came home about half-past ten on Thursday night, in last week. They were at supper at the time. Ever since the police had been on the search they had never drawn the blinds, and the son said afterwards that he had been watching them at supper. The son, on entering the house, said to his mother, , "Don't fret, mother, I have done nothing wrong. The only thing I have done wrong is to run away. I wish I had stood my ground and faced the truth." He said he had tramped 200 miles ; all the way home. As for the police, he looked many a one in the face, and not one had a suspicion who he was. He did not disguise himself. When he left Rixton he went towards Manchester, and then down through the Midlands to Worcester. He started from Worcester on Thursday 'morning, and tramped through Malvern,, Ledbury, and Hereford home. His accounr:. of the shooting was that he and Ella man were at their engines. Ellaman called out" Bring that thing, (the revolver) along, I want to have a look at it." Vaughan replied " I will in a few minutes." A minute or two afterwards he went across to Ellaman. who came a little way to meet him. Giving Ellaman the revolver, Vaughan said "It's all right ; there's no charge in it ; all the chambers are empty." He said he had been shorting starlings in the morning and he thought he had emptied all the chambers. He turned away for a moment, when all at once ho heard the report of a revolver and saw Ellaman staggering. Ellaman said" Oh dear, Fred, I've shot myself." Vaughan ran to him and caught him as he was falling, but Ellaman died on his arm. Prisoner was so frightened that he could not help to take the body away, and when he thought that he might be smpected of killing the man, he started off. On Friday, on the advice of his father, the son surrendered himself. The father added that Vaughan is not at all given to drink. REMOVAL OF THE PRISONER. Prisoner, who in the morning had been driven to Warrington from Leigh, in a trap, in charge of Mr. Weir, Was. afrer being brought before Captain Withington at the Oricisional '„Court House, retnoved in custody Of P.C. Whittinghain (Cdurity Police) and P.C. Chantler (Borough Police)to time Borough bridewell. There he was provided with dinner, and afterwards taken in the police van to the "Cheshire Lines Stations whence he was conveyed to Walton gaol.

At Sheffield Yesterday Matilda Wilson was prosecuttd bg the Socity for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, and committed for trial for the manslaughter of her daughter, aged three, by starvation. At Croydon, on Thursday afternoon, George Bowling was committed for trial on the charge of murdering Eliza Nightingale, his paramour, at Mitcham, on the 17th inst., by beating in her skull with a hammer. At the monchly meeting of the Preston Town Council on Thursday some statistics were presented with reference to the cost ot the protracted contest over the River and Dock Works Bills. It was alleged that the town had suffered to the extent of €lOO,OOO "by the action of the opposition outside the Council." A PARLI AMENTARY SECRETARY ON THE WAR PATH.— Mr. Walter Long, Parliamentary Secretary to the Local Government Board, addressing a meeting of Liberal Unionists irk Wiltshire, said that if the constituencies would speak out "members of the Unionist party would return after the recess prepared to deal much more strongly with the Opposition than they had dealt with them yet." The Liberal Unionists warmly applauded this intimation. Mr. Long also said that the Government were "not going to be frightened by the gibes and jeers of the Gladstonian rabble, who were hunting for a policy and for a leader." He" had a supreme contempt for them."
THE DROWNING OF TWO MEN IN A
PIT. FUNERAL OF THE VICTIMS.

On Sunday afternoon the remains of John Watsonl. Platt-st., and Thomas Forster, of the Travellers. Rest Inn, the victims of the drowning accident frt the pit at Orford-lane, which occurred last week - under circumstances previously reported, were interred in the Warrington Cemetery. The houses of the two deceased are situated near one another, and the funeral procession left at half-past one, Watson's hearse being first. Watson was a mem- ber of the Druids' Club and k orster a member of the Foresters. Both these clubs were largely repre- sented at the funeral, the members wearing their sashes, while the sashes of the deceased were hung on their respective hearses. Large crowds of people lined the road to the cemetery. and the scene in the - cemetery itself was of a touching nature.

div.head: LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR NEWTON DIVISION.
div.p: THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR NEWTON DIVISION.

The Executive of the Newton Division Liberal Association for some weeks past have had under ' consideration the selection Of a suitable candidate, - to represent the party at the next election in the constituency. Last week we reported a meeting of the Executive, and it was stated that the business - referred to political affairs in the division. It is novt generally understood that the name of Mr. J. F. Cheet- ham, of Staleybridge, was announced as the pro- bable candidate in the Liberal interest, and the. announcement was received with general satisfa- ction. The name of Cheetham is well-known throughout South West Lancashire, as the father of the probable Liberal candidate for Newton was formerly member of Parliament for old South-West Lancashire. prior to the Redistribution of Seats Bill dividing the con- stituency into several divisions. Mr. J. F. Cheetham himself has previously occupied a seat in the House of Commons as one of the representatives of the old North Derbyshire division. At an election for two seats .1' 1880, the result of the poll was as follows :—Cavendish (L), 3,410 ; Cheetham (L), 3,183 ; Arkwright (C). 2,936 ; Sidebottom (C), 2,718. In the case of Derby- shire the North Division was divided on the Redistribu tion Bill coming into force, and at the following election Mr. Cheetham decided to become a can- didate for the one seat alloted to the High Peak Division, and he was opposed by Major W. SidebottTn• The result of the contest—in 1885—was as under : side- bottom (C), 4,199; Cheetham (L), 4,190. Mr. Cheetham thus lost his seat in Parliament by the extremely low minority of nine votes. We understand that Mt. Cheetham has expressed favourable opinions in regard t 0 contesting the Newton Division, but up to the present he has not definitely consented to do so. Mr. Cheethalu is, we understand, at present on the Continent.
