div.p: WHITSUNTIDE, AT RUNCORN.

Of all festivals in the calendar none is anticipat with such pleasure, or is observed as a holiday more universally than Whitsuntide is in the to wn of Rua- corn. Preparations for the occasion are commenced by families weeks before it arrives and in two daYs fleeting pleasure the savings of a few months a e scattered. Whit Sunday would appear to be given up to a pilgrimage to Runcorn Hill and on Sunday morning and afternoon thousands of people wended their way to their native heath. As usual the Primitive Methodists held

CAMP MEETINGS there. The morning service in Greenway-road Chapel was dispensed with and a number of the members 01 the congregation led by their pastor, the Rev. C. Fine?, walked in procession to Runcorn Hill, singing hy:nns hearty fashion on the way. On arriving on the Hill, lir• Finch and several lay preachers delivered religious ad- dresses to the large crowd that assembled around then). A second camp meeting was held in the afternoon 0..15 while a large congregation listened to the preach hundreds wandered over the heath beyond the hearing of their impassioned pleading. The

PROCESSION OF CLUBS on Whit Monday was a very tame affair. Although there are about a dozen friendly societies established in the town, only the members of two of them demonstrated 00 the present anniversary. In fact the members only Pr°- fess to make a united display once in three yearn, and this was not the occasion for their effort. NeverthelesS the streets were well lined with spectators in order t 0 witness the peregrinations of the two clubs who did turn out. The Dukeo Club, established in 1790 in connection with the Bridgewater Canal, paraded the streets to thef music of the Mill Brow Brass Band, and in the ranks ° the 80 men who were in the procession were carried flags and bannerettes and the usual regalia was worn. div.head: CONSERVATISM IN NEWTON DIVISION.
div.p: CONSERVATISM IN NEWTON DIVISION.

DEMONSTRATION AT GOLBORNE PARK. Golborne Park, near Newton-le-Willows, was the scene of a Conservative demonstration on an exten- sive scale on Saturday afternoon. The gathering had been arranged under the auspices of the Gol- borne Polling District Conservative Club, and was participated, in by the Conservative organisations 'Within the district covered by the Newton Division Conservative Association. The proceedings were earned Out by a strong Committee of whom Mr. John Robinson was the chairman and Mr. Thomas Gregory • secretary, and owing to the hearty sup- Port accorded by the Chairman of the Golborne Club,the denaonstration,favoured with fine weather, Was a great success. Mr. W. J. Legh, lord of the Manor, had kindly granted the use of the park and grounds for the afternoon. The proceedings corn- Inenced with a procession from the Golberne Club to the Park, where elaborate preparations had been made for athletic competitions, football contests, dancing, &c. The Golborne and Haydock Brass Bands were present, and during the afternoon some thousands of persons attended. A largely attended meeting was held in the course of 'the proceedings. A platform had been erected under the shade of one of the large trees in the grounds, and here the chair was occupied by Mr. T. D. Grimke, J.P., who Was supported by Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., Mr. T. B. ,RoYden, M.P. for the West Toxeth Division of Liverpool; r• W. Bromley-Davenport, M.P. for the Macclesfield vivision of Cheshire; Messrs. T. H. Pearson J.P., T. J. Gillespie J.P., W. H. Arnott J.P., C.C., M. Brown- Westhead, R. Stone, C. 13. F. Borron, Wyndham Smith, A. 11. L. Evans, R. Owen, E. C. Cooper, J. Robinson, P. "'all, and others. At the request of the Chairman the audience sang the National Anthem and cheers were given for the Queen, in honour of her birthday. 41• T. W. Legh, Ml'., who was received with loud ?uJeers, proposed—" That this meeting begs to express As unabated confidence in her Majesty's present Unionist Government, and congratulates them most heartily upon the success of their policy, both at home and abroad, for as the result of the wise and statesmanlike manner in 'Which the affairs of the nation have been conducted ,unring their tenure of office, peace and prosperity have "een restored in Ireland, where all was confusion and anarchy, when they took up the reins of Government; trade has greatly improved, taxation has been greatly reduced, and we are at peace with all the world. This tneeting wishes also to recerd its cordial approval of the Z°Posals contained in the local taxation (Customs and xoise) duties bill, with regard to the licensing question." After th some introductory observations, he remarked that ""ere was held not long ago in Golborne what was described as a great Liberal meeting. That meeting was addressed by a Parnellite member of Parliament— r- joseph Nolan—who was not particularly die- •lmguished, and was one of those who represented reload by keeping carefully away from it. • Laughter.) But Mr. Nolan, who came down to preach °lne Rule in the Newton Division, happened to have ".een the same person who had introduced into the House 14 Commons the dynamiters, Melville and Huskins, now 'anguishing in gaol. Mr. Nolan had asserted that he did !lot know that those men were dynamiters, and probably that was true ; he was unfortunate in his friendships, but at the same time, it had transpired before the House ,„‘3l Commons Committee of Inquiry that he was the ~,,-“,aPeron of the daughters of another illustrious dyne- *Ver, General Millen. Mr. Nolan was then the member - Parliament who came to ask them why he (Mr. Legh) oPposed the Land Purchase Bill of Mr. Gladstone, 'nilst he supported that of Mr. Balfour. He had no objection to answering the question. When Mr. Glad- 13iti0118's bill was introduced he was not in Parliament— if he had been he would have opposed it. 17, Gladstone proposed upon a perfectly illusory security sPend £200,000,000 in buying out Insh landlords, and rscheme was condemned, not only by his oppments, bY his friends. On the other hand, Mr. Balfour, by an _i ligeniong arrangement, obviated the liability to the ritsh tax payer, whilst he required a much smaller sum. Zilch was the kind of criticism their opponents used. 4erred VGLeY kept Home Rule in the back-ground. They pre- to go into any other question. At the present I,nornent the pro;losals for plundering publicans— 'Shame ")—were a far more alluring topic. Putting V 9 Point shortly he would say that they were fighting in ns last matter on a question of confiscation or compen- aiation. The compensationists said that when a man was `'agar...,ed in a legitimate business he had a right to be protected, and that to take away his business when he tfitad done nothing to justify such a course was m0n- ..,„1:9u51Y unfair and unjust. (Hear, hear.) The confis- T 1 onists, on the other hand, looked upon the publican a child of the devil, as an enemy of the human race r;no ought to be thankful of anything short of hanging. V.4maughter.) The compensation which ought to be allowed was, in their opinion, something equivalent to penal Be: v. dude, Unfortunately no question seemed to arouse aujallch bitterness as this question of temperance versus All ought to admire the efforts of the temperance •he;r:ners, and be themselves temperance reformers alp 4, hut he contended that the Government and their 0,7 unporters as a whole had the temperance cause at heart, "nd that to extinguish licenses with money raised by an o extra tax n intoxicants was a step in the direction of natra r Perance reform. (Hear, hear.) He did not believe I'a t the opponents of the Government had any genuine in Pathy with the cause of temperance. He believed "leY would support anything which tended to embarrass

the Government, but personally he intended to give the Government every support in his power. (Cheers.)— Mr. 'T. B. Boyden, M.P., in seconding the resolution, alluded to the great interest which Mr. Legh took in questions affecting the Newton division, and said the Unionist party was determined to persevere in their measures in spite of the persistent obstruction of their opponents. Comparing the present position of the coun- try with its position when the Government took office, he printed to the improvement of trade and the freedom from war scares which had attended the accession of the Conservatives to power; and, turning to the question of Ireland, said a wave of prosperity and of renewed indus- try was passing over that country, and he believed that when Mr. Bailout's land purchase bill became law Ireland would enter upon a period of long and uninter- rupted prosperity. (Cheers.) In regard to the licensing proposals, he asserted that the action of the Govern- ment proved them to be desirous of furtheling the tem- perance movement. (Hear, hear.) The Radicals said much about the temperance cause at the hustings, but they did nothing for it in the House. The Government, on:the contrary, was carrying out its pledges,believing at the same time no good woald be done by robbing any man. I Let them give credit to the Government for dropping the twaddle about temperance, and for tackling the question with a determination to do what was right. (Cheers.)— Mr. Bromley Davenport, M.P., in supporting the resolu- tion claim d that not only had the Government passed much useful legislation in the face of determined obstruction, but that they had improved every depart- ment of the administration. Mr. J. Robinson (Golborne), afterwards mcved a vote of thanks to Mr. Legh, M.P., for his services in Parliament and a hope was expressed that he would long be spared to represent the Newton Division. He said the Golborne Conservatives were fully determined, to again return him victorious if he had an • opponent at the next election.—Mr. Silcock (Golborne) seconded the resolution, which was supported by Mr. M. Brown-Westhead who had an enthusiastic reception. He urged the importance of continued and hearty, co-opera- tion among the Unionists of the division. The thanks were heartily accorded, and Mr. Legh, M.P., briefly ack- nowledged the compliment. On the motion of Mr. W. Arnott, J.P. C.C., seconded by Mr. A. H. L. Evans a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr.. W. J. Legh, lord of the manor, for granting the use of the park. Messts. Boyden, Bromley-Davenport, and M. B. West- head responded. A cordial vote of thanks was paid to the Chairman on the motion of Mr. T. H. Pearson, J.P., seconded by Mr. Waddington. '
WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.
ANNUAL REPORT.

The report of this institution for the year 1889 states that, the college is doing an important work, and doing it with success. The students for the year n.umbered 101, but one left through ill-health, and the remaining hundred acquitted themselves admirably at the Government examination for certificates. The list is as follows: Ist Class. 2nd Class. 3rd Class. Total. Juniors Seniors The seniors' list in 1888, when they were juniors, was :- Ist Class. 2nd Class. 3rd Class. Total. 4 In freehand, 23 students passed in the first class, and 19 in the second ; in geometry 33 passed; in perspective, 32 in the first class, and five in the second ; in black- board 27 ; end in light and shade, 19. Thirteen students gained their full drawing certificate. In the science of physiography, all who sat for the elementary ex inaination passed, twenty-seven in the first class, twenty-four in the second ; in the advanced, four passed in the first class, and eleven in the second. The grant for passes in the Science and Art examina- tions amounted to £l5B. Nineteen students obtained the South Kensington local diploma for cookery, by which they are qualified to teach that subject in elementary schools The senior students were examined in music by Sir John Stainer, on Thursday, September 26th. and passed most creditably, thirty-eight out of forty-eight being marked "excellent," seven " good," and three fair." On Friday, October 17th, Dr. Fitch went over the college' addressed the students and met the Committee. To the latter he communicated his opinions on the staff and work of the college in full detail. His judgment on the conduct of the institution reflected the greatest pos- sible credit on the Principal, Rev. Morley Stevenson, of whom he spoke in terms of high praise. The work of the students, and their character and tone, were allthat could be desired. He, however, again expressed his regret that there was not a recreation room worthy of all the other appointments, which were admir- able. The Queen's scholarship examination was held in the first week of July. There were one hundred and sixty- eight candidates. Fifty-one new students were adrmitted into the college in January, 1890. The three exhibitions offered by the Committee were gained by Mary Annie Charlton, Stamford-st. Board School, Bolton.; Ellen Jane Pierce, Llandegai School, Bangor; and Mary Houghton, the Mount School, Warrington.

BOATING FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.

A sad boating fatality occurred on the Mersey at Warrington on Sunday evening, when one young Man lost his life; and twd others had narrow escapes. Prom particulars that have been gathered, and from the evidence given at the inquest, it appears that the men, John Doyle, Robert Shields and Curheth Woodhead, All tailors by trade, era 3 ployed by the Grand Clothing Hall Compaay, Bridge- street, hired a boat at: Wilderspool, and went for a /row up the 'river-. They had passed under Warrington - Bridge,an. l were rounding the bend near Messfs. Roberts, Dale, anJ Go.'s wharf, when ribvle, whb was rowing, missed his stroke, and the boat capsized, the ocetniants being thrown into the river. The accident was 'witnessed _ by a number of people on the bank, and assistance rendered.. Two of the men, Robert Shields and Curbeth Woodhead, were rescued, but Doyle was not taken from - the water until after the lapse-of nearly a quarter of an hour. Under the direction of Dr. Peacocke, who had reached the scene, the usual treatment in such cases was applied by the police, but without avail. me deceased, Who was a native of Dublin, was 20 years of age, and lodged at 68, Iloward-st., Sankey Bridges. THE INQUEST

On Thursday afternoon Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy- coroner for South-West Lancashire, held an intiuiry at the Higher Seven Stars Inn, Bridge-st., Warrington, as to the cinitunstances qf the death of Doyle. Robert William Burchenshaw, 68, Howard-st., was the first witness called. He deposed that the body viewed bY the jury was that of James Doyle, who lived at 68, Howard-st., Sankey Bridges, and'was a tailor. He was hetwe.en nineteen and twenty years of age. Witness saw deceased at 4.30 on Sunday afternoon' when he was sober and was apparently in good health. Thomas Brooks, apprentice boiler-maker, 18, Stephen- aon-st., Warrington, said that, on Sunday afternoon last some men hired a boat from him at about twenty Minutes to five. There were three men, and they hired a rowing boat, at Wharf-st. The deceased was one of them. They had got about fifty xards from the hiring Place when one man missed his stroke, and lost his oar. The boat went broadside on the stream, the three men fell over in the water, and the boat capsized. There "were only two oars. Two of the men swam towards the Cheshire shore and one to the Lancashire shore. ,Tvvo of the men landed safely on the Cheshire shore. Vitness was satisfied that it was an accidental capsizing of the boat. Witness thought that the water at the spot in question would be about eight feet deep. Deceased had hold of an oar, but let it go, and sank. James Woods, Orchard-st., Warrington, a shoemaker, aid that on Sunday afternoon he saw three men in a at. Ile then described how the accident occurred, Corroborating the evidence of the previous witness. De- ceased, he said, was about twelve minutes in the water. The Coroner said that there were several other wit- nesses, but he thought that the jury had got as much as they could get to know of the matter. If they were anxious to hear any other witnesses, he was quite will- Inspector Spinks said that neither of the other two men /vho were with the boat had been properly'well since the

accident sh.; "Ad pperle. The Coroner said that outsiders often knew most of a Matter, and he had no doubt that those who saw the ?ccurrence had told them all that was to be told. He 'bought that there was puly one conclusion to be arrived at—that the deceased was drowned by the upsetting of the boat. Inspector Spinks : Dr. Feacocke arrived on the scene, lk,pd Sergeant Rowbothain and two constables who were l'nere tried artificial respiration for 45 minutes, but with- Out avail. The Coroner said that the poisonous nature of thv water Would be against it. He thought it would be safe to ePlne to the conclusion that the man was accidentally drowned. The jury returned a verdict to that effect. A SCENE. During the progress of the inquest, a commotion was heard outside the room in which it was held, and sud- denly thedoor was burst open, and two or three police- nlen, who were struggling with a civilian, tumbled into the room, and put a sudden stop to the proceedings. 'r h e jurymen rose to their -feet in excitement, and the coroner called upon them to resume their seats and remain quiet. The man was struggling desparately th the police, and exclaimed that he, too, should have Peen drowned. Finally he was forced out of the room !,nd pacified, after which he was taken home by his .rriends. It transpired that his name was Woodhead, and 'hat he was one of the men who occupied the boat. He Lad been warned to attend as a.witness, and it is thought that brooding over the sad affair had turned his brain. •

div.head: ARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS AT , WIDNES. "A " COMPANY CLASS-FIRING.
div.p: ARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS AT , WIDNES. "A " COMPANY CLASS-FIRING.

_ The members of" A" Company of the Warrington Volunteers, had a 'successful meeting at the Widnes rifle range on Saturday, which was the day, appointed by battalion orders for the performance of their 3rd class firing. Five prizes, of 7s. 6d., 55., 3s. 6d., 2s. 6d., and is. 6d., respectively, were offered for competition as an encouragement for good shooting and for the men to attend. The men assembled at the Drill Hall at 1.45, and proceeded, under the command of the adjutant (Captain Adam) and Captain Buckton, from the Central Station by the 2.5 p.m train to Widnes, commencing the shoot- ing shortly before three o'clock and finishing at 7.0. The weather was fi.ne, and there was less smoke than usual, owing, perhaps, to the approach of Whit-week. There was a strong wind blow- ing across the range from the east, rendering high scoring very difficult. Thirty-five men of the com- pany attended and fired, this being a larger number than any previously obtained on these occasions. Colonel Twentyman, C. 8., who is in command of the regimental district, visited the range during the afternoon, and watched the shooting for some time. On leaving he expressed his high appreciation of the scoring. Twenty- eight of the men passed into 2nd class, and will therefore be eligible to proceed to Altcar (to-day) Saturday to fire at the longer ranges. Each man fired—Five rounds kneeling at 100 yards, five rounds standing at 100 yards, five rounds kneeling at 200 yards, five rounds lying down at 300 yards. div.p: THE RELIGIOUS CONTROVERSY.

I see by your editorial remarks that I am ex- clud:xl from taking any further part in the religious con- troversy (Mr. Williamson having the exclusive right of replying to Messrs. Foulkes. Hargreaves, Truth, and Dis- senter), I am reluctantly compelled to caneel the manus- cript of letter No 2. which I intended to send to your paper this week for publication. Thanking you for the liberal manner in which you published the correspond- ence on both sides of the question.—l remain, dear sir, yours very truly, Runcorn, 28th ay, 1890.
RANGATIRA.
THE ORXNGE PEEL NUISANCE.

Sir,—As the orange peel season is now in full swing I allow me once again to relate the following: Walking one day in Victoria-st., Manchester,l saw a gentleman throw a piece of orange peel on the roadway. I went and re- quested him not to do so. He said he never threw it on the pavement, but thought it all right to cast it on the carriage way. I showed him that it was the more dangerous place of the two, as people crossing in a hurry, and in front of a conveyance, or getting off a tramcar, might slip, be run over, and have to be taken to the Infirmary. He saw the danger, and promised to do what I suggested, viz., in future when he ate oranges in the streets to put the peel in his pocket, and throw it in the fire when he returned home ; and I hope that all who read this, and eat oranges and other fruits in the streets of Warrington, Widnes, St. Helens, Earlestown, Newton, Runcorn, Chester, Manchester, Liverpool, London, and wherever your influential journals circulate, will fellow that gentleman's example. Many may read this who do not eat fruit in the streets, who do so whilst travelling by rail—to all such I would suggest—take with you a small basket or bag for the re- mains of your refreshment, and do not throw out of the carriage windows the fruit peeling and other debris of your repast, the empty lemonade bottles, &e., to the endangering nf the lives of the platelayers, and others at work on the line, who might slip en the former in avoid- ing the latter, and be knocked down and killed ny the passing express. Many years ago I removed from the path on the Torrs Rock, Ilfracombe, a quantity of peel that had carelessly been left there; had anyone slipped on it they might have been dashed on the rocks below. I sometime ago had a letter from a gentleman who had narrowly escaped being run over and trampled to death by horses in Fleet-st., through stepping on peel; he also saw three other cases, one of which was fatal ; and I sometime age saw a gentleman nearly have a fall through the same thing. People may say that "it is the children that do it ; " then why do not the parents teach them better? A little care is better than a broken leg, or loss of life. That prevention is better than cure, and example better than precept, is the opinion of your correspondent. —Yours, &C., Sale, Cheshire, May 21st, 1890.

div.head: ALEXANDER WADDELL.
div.p: ALEXANDER WADDELL.
ROMAN CATHOLICISM.

Sir,—l beg to thank you for your kind indulgence in granting me permission to write a few parting lines to my friend " A Dissenter," and the host of other con- tributors to your valuable paper, both for and against the Catholic Church argument which has been going on now for some weeks. Arguments followed on the limes presented to you by some of your correspondents are not likely to lead to any satisfactory results. Raving given an explanation of what I thoroughly believe, and which is the teaching of the Catholic Church, on the Points of dispute raised, I find that my arguments are met partly by abuse and partly by erroneous contradic- tions. If anyone take the trouble to review my previous explanations they will see ample evidence to satisfy themselves of the veracity of my statements. The following are the real facts. Your correspondent, a " Dissenter," has made the following statements, to which I append an answer, and which statements I think have fully proved to be untrue. Ist. That we Catholics adore images, saints, relics, &c. Answer. This fact the Catholic Church does not teach, neither do I believe. 2nd. That we make nse of saints' symbols, calveries, crucifixes, Ste., which distract us from Christ. Answer. No; but as human nature is always tending to go astray from Christ, we respect these objects with a relative honour which reminds us of the "Eternal One," and to excite our devotion and reverence into leading a good and a holy life, by keeping the Commandments. 3rd. That we worship the Virgin Mary, and put her in the place of God. Answer. No, we only give her relative honour, but we do not give her Divine honour, which belongs to God alone. There were passages in the other letters which I should like to have answered, and which to fair-minded persons might have caused perplexity, but as my letters were addressed to " Dissenter," I did not think it was my duty to reply to all. I may, however, explain one, viz., the Greek word " Latria" "ke other worship (there are different kinds of worship) ~,ay be absolute or relative. 4th. That we follow traditional doctrines. Answer. Yes, but I may remind him that tradition existed before the Bible. sth". That we are fcrbidden to read the Bible. Answer. No, but we are encouraged to do so. As a matter of fact your correspondews all inveigh against the Catholic Church withcut having in the least attempted to go into the other side of the 'question, in fact, all their argu- ments go to prove that which everybody knows. The next time your correspondent " A Dissenter," or the others, make such a fruitless attempt on argument I would advise them strongly to forecast what their opponents are likely to admit and what they will deny. They will then have a chance of proving them. The letters of" Bedtail " and " Rangatira" have a certain amount of truth in them, but they were not all Gospel. I point to one thing, viz., that they were in the same opinion on these points as all other Catholics are, though, perhaps, some are not capable of instructing others. It shows plainly that the Catholics as a body are not such a lot of fools as your correspondents would make them appear. They know where to draw the line as to what is idolatry and what is not, without the incoherent re- marks and public erroneous statements like what has been published in the columns of your very valuable paper. These facts are practically unknown to many Protestants, but which every Catholic child learns in his Catechism. Your correspondents may be sincere in searching after truth, hut if they are invincibly ignorant of the truth, and they cannot see light in its true colours. then I say, and it is taught, that good Protestants will get a better chance of going to heaven than bad Catholics. This being so, why are these public charges (which are not true) made against the Catholic Church more than against any other ? It were far better for religion, for country, and for selves, if a more charitable feeling were exliibited to- wards one another. There are .in Runcorn some happy feelings existing amongst all classes. Let us hope they will continue and leave these important points of dispute to be settled by those who are able to instruct us. s;) wishing your cotrespondents good-bye, I must now devote my time, intellect, and energy, to some other im- portant work which may help in the general improve- ment of our people, and remain, yours truly, THOMAS WILLIAMSON. 263, Bridge-st., Birkenhead, 27th May, 1890.

STEAM NAVVIES ON THE SHIP CANAL

This week we give an illustration of the German steam navvy, a machine which has done and is still uoing a useful work on the Ship Canal. It will be seen that this navvy is more of the style of a dredger, but there are different types of the machine,so.ne to excavate the side of a cutting which lies below the rails on which the navvy stands, and others to scoop a rising face of soil. The machine when at work is placed on rails, and inside these rails, and parallel with them, are laid the transport rails on which the locomotives run that drag the trains of tip-wagons, as seen in the larger cut. The buckets are made to run on a powerful rack depend- ing from the top of the machine, and as each bucket strikes the ground and is filled with soil the machinery forces it up another rack and the soil is then tipped into the wagons, which run through a a kind of shed that forms the framework of the machine, the actual working portion of which is elevated. These excavators are made by the Lubeck Machine Construction Co., of Lubeck, Germany. They are reckoned to be capable of displacing as much as 2,600 cubic yards of light soil, or about 1,960 yards of tenacious ground in a working day of ten hours.

THE PURCHASE OF THE WATERWORKS. THE FINAL OFFER OF VIE CORPORATION. The General Purposes Committee of the Warring- ton Town Council have passed the following resolu- tion :—That the following terms of purchase as finally arranged with the Directors of the Water- works Co. at the interview had on the 28th May, 1890, be agreed to and adopted, and that the Town Clerk be instructed to make a final offer of such terms to the Company :- 1. The consideration for the purchase shall be a sum equivalent to 30 years purchase of the maximum statu- tory annualdividends upon the present paid up capital of the company, that is to say, £4-i per cent upon £40,000 preference stock, £lO per cent upon 3,000 shares of £lO each, £74, per cent upon 1,500 shares of £lO each, and £7 per cent upon 3,000 shares of £lO each. 2. All debts and liabilities of the Uoinpany, including the mortgage or bond debt, remaining unpaid or un- satisfied at the time of the transfer, shall be taken over as then existing, and be paid and satisfied by the Cor- poration. 3. The Corporation shall take over all the assets of the Company, except a sum of money representing the amount of revenue and profits from earnings undivided at the time of transfer, in which sum is to included, such portion of the Company's Reserve Fund as consists of appropriations of revenue. 4. The Corporation shall issue annuities to the share- holders in respect of their shares or stock charged and secured according to the usual practice of Parliament, such annuities being equal in amount to the maximum statutory dividends upon such shares or stock respec- tively. 5. The annuities issued in respect of the preference stock shall not be redeemable before the first day of January, 1921, except by agreement with the proprietors thereof. 6. Every preference stockholder shall be entitled to the option of receiving, in lieu of an annuity' an annuity bond, conditioned to be redeemed by the Corporation within one year from the date of transfer by payment in cash of a sum equal to 30 years purchase, such option to be declared within three months after the passing of the Act. 7. Subject as aforesaid, the Ccrporation to have power to redeem all or any annuities on giving six months notice, and on payment in cash of a sum equal to 30 years' purchase; but the power of redemption not to be exercised in any case before the first day of January, 1896, except by agreement with the proprietors. 8. The Corporation shall pay to the Company at or before the date of transfer, a sum of £3,000, to be placed at the disposal of the directors, and applied by them in payment of the costs, charges, and expenses incurred by the Company, of, and incident to, the Corporation Bill, the negotiations, the transfer of the undertaking, and the winding up of the affairs of the Company, and also in compensations and gratuities to the Com- pany's officers and servants. 9. In the event of Mr. John Ross, the secretary and engineer of the Company, agreeing to continue his ser- vices as manager of the undertaking, the Corporation shall take him over on the same terms, as to position and emolument-e, as at present, and he shall not be liable to clismis;al or removal from his office for a period of four years' from the data of transfer, save only for miscon- duct and incapacity, but he himself may terminate the engagement by six months' notice, to be given to the Corporation at any time. 10. All other persons in the service of the Company, shall, if willing to continue their services to the Corpor- ation, be taken over on the same terms as to position and emoluments as at present, and shall not be liable to dismissal or removal for a period of two years from the date of transfer, save only for misconduct or incapacity, but may themselves terminate the engagement by one month's notice, to be given to the Corporation at any time. 11. 'The transfer shall take effect on and from the 26th day of March, 1891. The Corporation shall take over the Company's undertaking as a going concern, and shall pay to the Company at the date of the transfer a sum in cash equal to the amount of the water rents and all other income of the undertaking then accrued, due, and remaining unpaid (subject to deduction in re- spect of had debts or sums irrecoverable, if any such there shall be), and shall after making such payment, 'he entitled to receive and collect such water rents and income. 12. The minute books of proceedings of share- holders, directors, and committees, and all other books and documents which are not reason- ably necessary for the conduct of the business of the undertaking, shall not be transferred to the Corpor- ation, but shall be retained by the Company. Any difference or dispute with respect to such books or docu- ments shall he settled by an arbitrator, to be agreed upon between the Corporation and the Company, previous to the passing of the Bill through Committee of the House of Commons, whose name shall be inserted in the Bill, and whose cecision shall be final. 13. The Corporation Bill shall be altered and amended, and new clauses inserted therein, as may be required by the Company or their Parliamentary agents, so as to embody therein the foregoing terms of purchase, and to give effect thereto, and also to provide for the dissolu- tion of the Company,and the winding up of its affairs as may be desired by the Company. The above offer is made subject to an examination by the Corporation of the Company's property and accounts. it being of course understood that the examination is to take place under the conditions and restrictions provi- sionall7,- arranged at the interview with your Board on the 16th April last.

PROFESSOR BOYD DAWKINS' REPORT.

At the request of the Corporation, and in view of the proposed purchase of the Warrington Waterworks Com- pany's undertaking by the Corporation, both Professor Boyd Dawkins, F.R.S., F.R.G.5.., Assoc. Inst. C.E., and Professor of Geology in Owen's College, and Mr. Charles E. De Rance, Assoc. Inst. C.E., F.G.S., F.R.G.S., have presented reports as to the water supply from the Win- wick wells of the Waterworks Company, dealing particu- larly with the question of the probable permanence of thesupplv. Below we give full reprints of these reports, which, apart altogether front their important bearing up- on the scheme of waterworks' purchase, are full of in- teresting !oral information.

Professor Boyd Dawkins says: "Having been requested to advise the Mayor and Corporation of Warrington as to the permanence of the supply of water from the Win- wick Pumping Station, and as to the probable effect o working the coal-measures under the Winwick area, beg to present the following report:—

div.head: WATE U-BEA RING ROCKS.
div.p: THE WATE U-BEA RING ROCKS.

- The strata in the Winwick area of supply consist of new red sandstone, highly charged with water, and covered irregularly with superficial sands. They form the two lower divisions of the Bunter or Lower Triassic Group, Nos. land 2 of the following sections : Thickne,s. Wells. 3. Upper mottled sandstone sto 600 feet ... 2. Pebble beds 975 feet 5 Bootle. 600 feet Whiston.
Lower_mottled_sandstone

The pebble beds in this district are at least 500 feet thick. In the deep boring at Bootle they are no less than 975 feet in thickness ; their exact thickness in this district remains to be proved. The lower mottled sandstone No. 1, is more than 800 feet in thickness at Whiston, near St. Helens. All these three rocks form one water-bearing system.

THE POSITION IN THE ROCKS OF THE WELLS AT WINWICK. The wells at Winwick begin near the top of the pebble beds No. 2, and the bottom of the borings, according to the data, published by Mr. Boult, in 1876, is 353 feet from the surface. They draw, therefore, upon only the upper third of the total thickness of the new red sand- stone, which in that place is not less than 1,000 feet, the lower two-thirds having not hitherto been used for pur- poses of water supply.

div.head: PERMIAN MARLS FORM A WATER-TIGHT BARRIER.
div.p: PERMIAN MARLS FORM A WATER-TIGHT BARRIER.

Below these new red sandstone rocks come (B) the im- pervious Permian marls, and (A) the Permian sand- stones irregular in thickness, and covering the eroded edges of the coal-measure rocks below, and separating them from the water-bearing new red sandstone (I). The marls, B, form a water-tight barrier, which prevents the new red sandstone water from getting into the coal- measures, excepting at the edges of the coal-field, where the sandstones have been faulted against the coal-seams and associated rocks.

div.head: EFFECT OF MINING ON WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: EFFECT OF MINING ON WATER SUPPLY.

The coal-measures crop out at the surface four miles to the north-west of the pumping station, and occur at Witiwick at a depth of not less than from twelve to fifteen hundred feet. If, in the future, they are worked in this area, it is very unlikely that the workings will affect the new red sandstone water, because of the Permian Marl (B), which is sandwiched between the two rocks. It will be impossible—even if shafts be sunk through the new red sandstone—into the coal-measures to work the coal without tubbing out the water.

div.head: DRAINAGE AREA AND YIELD OF WATER.
div.p: DRAINAGE AREA AND YIELD OF WATER.

The area of water-bearing rocks commanded by the Winwick site is very large, extending as far north as the coal-measures of Ashton-in-Makerfield, .and Parr Moss, and including Lowton, Kenyon, and Croft. It amounts to not less than 21 square miles, which taking the mean annual rainfall at 30 inches, should yield from seven-and- a-half to eight-and-a-half million _gallons per day. The prescnt yield is said to la) one million gallons. In 1876 it was, according to Mr. Boult, eight hundred thousand gallons from one well and bore hole. The yield might be largely increased by sinking into the subterranean reser- vol., Which exists in the new red sandstone, and which as I have already pointed out, is untouched in this spot. On this point it must be noted that theyield at Whiston, in 1874, from the lower mottled sandstone (I), from an area of percolation of about one-tenth of that of Winwick, was .ne million gallons per day. The supply may also be largely increased by sinking wells in the new red sandstone rocks, south of Winwick, and nearer War- rington.

div.head: GENERAL RESULTS OF ENQUIRY.
div.p: GENERAL RESULTS OF ENQUIRY.

I am, therefore, after examining all the evidence bear- ing on the new red sandstone water, of opinion—firstly, that the supply from the Winwick area is permanent; secondly, that it may be very largely increased by further works, judiciously placed ; and lastly, that there is no reason to suppose that it will be affected by mining oper- ations in the future. MR. DE RANCE'S REPORT.

Mr. De Rance reports as follows:—" In accordance with your request that I should report to your Board, as to the capabilities of the Warrington Waterworks Company's Undertaking, to provide a larger supply of water of good quality than at present, should the population of Warrington largely increase, and that I should further consider whether the present or future yield is likely to be affected by the possible working of coal. in the neighbourhood of the present or future works, I beg to offer the following result of my study of the facts that have been brought to my knowledge, as regards this district, and the conclusions that I draw from them :—I have been acquainted with the district for fifteen years, and I carried out the Government Geological Survey of the superficial deposits, or drift, over the greater part of the area surrounding the works.

THE WIN WICK 'WELLS. As secretary of the Underground Water Committee of the British Association, the details of every boring made in this and other districts come before me, and in 1880, I published the following details of the results obtained by the Winwick well and boring :—Level of surface of pumping station about 110 feet above ordnance datum, or mean tide-level at Liverpool.—Well 127 feet five inches in depth, with a diameter of nine feet.—Boring carried to 412 feet from the surface, diameter 14 inches. „ DEPTH ju feet

Previous to the execution of the well and boring, two other wells had been sunk to a depth stated to be 150 feet, or" 40 0. D." (forty feet below Ordnance Datum). From this an unlined bore-hole was carried to 212 feet below it, or " 252 0. D." This bore-hole from falls be- came choked, in its lower 50 feet, its diameter was 18 inches. The two wells were one within the engine- house, the other immediately outside it, at a depth of 50 feet from the surface, a large storage reservoir is excav- ated out of the sand-stone, this chamber throws the two wells into one, from this depth to the bottom. The No. 3 well is distant from the twin-wells, 80 feet, and is connected with them by a tunnel in the rock. The bore- hole in the now well is lined, and a tube is carried up, above the level of the water in the well, the water some- times standing in the bore-hole, 50 feet above the level of the water in the well. The wells and borings at Win- wick in 1878 were capable of giving an average supply of half-a-million gallons daily, and it was anticipated that the new works then contemplated, and since carried out, would yield another quarter-of-a-million. These works consisted of a tunnel driven at a uniform level from the pumping station, to a field near the Spa well, a distance of 1,200 yards, in a south-easterly direc- tion ; the work was carried from four shafts,number one
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 31, 1890

being at the Winwick pumping station, and number four near the Spa well, from which headings were driven in various directions. The surface level of the ground at the number four shaft is about 45 feet above Ordnance Datum, or about 65 feet lower than the surface at num- ber one. South and north of the pumping station are quarries in the pebble beds, dipping south or south-east at low angles ; pebbles are fairly numerous, but were not found in sinking Nos. 1 and 2 shafts; the strata con- sisted of soft red moulding sand, most easily worked, resembling the mottled sandstone division of the Bunter, but it probably was only a soft bed in the pebble beds. These were well marked in the No. 3 shaft, where the rock was hard, compact, contained many pebbles, and was traversed by mild planes of current-bedding. Num- erous pebbles also occurred in No. 4 shaft, but the rock was not so hard. At the depth of 90 feet a very strong spring was met with, which was probably that supply- ing the Spa well. which shortly later entirely failed, and the adjacent Spa brook has been very largely dimin- ished in quantity.

in a suitable situation, of which there are several, the present supply could easily be doubled. I see no reason to suppose the present supply will dinainish, without any further works being carried out, and I see from the chemical evidence given before the House of Lords, in 1878, that the water obtained is absolut -Ay pure. I see no reason to doubt that it will always re nain a first-class supply, both as regards quality and quantity."

div.head: MEETING OF THE WATER WORKS COMPANY.
div.p: MEETING OF THE WATER WORKS COMPANY.

. An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Water Works Company has been called for the 18th of June, for the purpose of considering the proposal made by the Corporation for the purchase of the Com- pany's undertaking, and, "if it shall be so resolved, of approving such proposal and authorising the directors of the Company to accept the same, and to take any measures which may be necessary for carrying it into effect."

div.head: CRICKET: THE AUSTRALIANS BEAT
div.p: CRICKET: THE AUSTRALIANS BEAT
LANCASHIRE.

Play was confirmed at Old Trafford, Manchester, yesterday. A lot of rain fell on Thursday night and the sun shon out yesterday morning, so the wicket fav- oured the bowlers immensely and the Lancashire bats- men were speedily dismissed. Turner and Ferris shared the bowling. Sugg left at 56. Hornbv caught at slip at. 59, and Ward taken long-off. Turner in successive overs then bowled Kemp, Holden, and Watson, and Mold was run out, and the innings closed at 12 20 for 78 runs. Turner took six wickets for 23 runs. Wanting 238 to save an innings defeat, Lancashire followed on at 1240. Hereby and Briggs went in and scored 32 runs from eight overs before Turner dismissed the Lancashire captain. The beneficial influence of the roller soon wore off. Sugg skied a ball between the wickets, and after Trumble displaced Ferris at 52. Albert Ward, Bar- low, and Kemp were dismissed ; five for 55. A catch at wicket dismissed Brigas at 65, and Holden, Frank Ward, Mold, and Whiteside getting out, the Australians won by an innings and 155 runs. Score : AUSTRALIANS. First Innings. Second Innings. div.head: ARREST OF A SUPPOSED ..DYNAMITARD.
div.p: ARREST OF A SUPPOSED ..DYNAMITARD.

Joseph Kaiser, anarchist, and follower of Johann Most, has been arrested on suspicion for attempting to blow up the Haymarket Statute erected in memory of the police- men killed by bombs thrown by the rioters at a pro- claimed meeting five years ago. For this crime the anarchists Fischer, Lingg, and Parsons were sentenced to the gallows. IMPENDING GREAT STRIKE OF COLLIERS. The notices to terminate contracts at the collieries inl the Blaenavon, Cyfarfa, Tredeg,ar, and Dowlais districts terminate to-day. The enginemen and stokers contend that a further advance in wages is now due, and have I also given notice for a rednetion in the hours of labour. A strike that will affect 10,000 miners is impending. Later intelligence says that a deputation representing the Dowlais Colliery enginemen having waited on Mr. Henry Martin, colliery manager, he has agreed to concede an advance of n per cent. to continue until theend of June. The men have consented to resume work, pending settle- ment of ether demands. A QCARTETTE OF CANDIDATES. Mr. Harry Frederick Pollock, of Kirklingtonhall, Newark, has consented to become the Unionist candidate for Spalding Division. He is a Liberal Unionist. Mr. Alf. Tupton, ,brother of Lord Flothfield, was on Thursday chosen as the Liberal candidate for North Westmoreland at the next general election, and Mr. Edward Colston, of Devizes, has been selected as the Conservative candidate for the Thornbury Division of Gloucestershire, in the place of Lord Dunsany, who will not seek re-election. It is understood that Mr. T. Gibson has consented to con- test the Heywood division of Lancashire at the next election as a Conservative.

div.head: NEWFOUNDLAND AGITATION.
div.p: THE NEWFOUNDLAND AGITATION.

News from Halifax states that the steamer liarlaw, which arrived there on Thursday. from St. George's Bay, reports that after the French cruiser Indre compelled the inhabitants to take up their herring nets the Frenchmen were somewhat surprised by the arrival of the British' screw sloop Pelican, which, however, evidently acting under orders, did not interfere ia any way. The inha- bitants afterwards assembled in large numbers, and, amid scenes of great enthusiasm, resolved not to pay any import duties until they were properly protected. Among those who carried the resolution were the leading lawyers, clergymen, and merchants, and it is extremely probable that the entire 12,000 inhabitants for seven hundred miles along the coast will follow their example EXCITING SCENE AT LIVERPOOL LANDING- STAGE.

_ An occurrence took place yesterday forenoon, on the George's Landing-stage, which caused the greatest excitement among the large crowd who witnessed it. As the Woodside ferryboat was approaching the stage a young man, having the appearance of an excursionist, was noticed to jump from (he boat into the river. The tide was running out strongly at the time, and he was carried under the paddle-wheel of the boat. The occur- rence was noticed by one of the crew of a Seacombe ferryboat, who gallantly jumped-into the river with the , object of reselling the excursionist. With the aid of a lifebuoy which was thrown to him the ferry boatman , swain towards the excursionist and made a grab at him, but only got hold of his hat, the man being carried away with the tid6, and soon after disappearing. The ferry- man at- this point lost hold of the buoy, and being exhausted by his strugglas was also nearly carried away. Some of his fellow-boatmen, seeing his perilous position, got into the water with a life-buoy to rescue him. While he was about sinking they fortunately got hold of his hands and dragged him on board the boat. The brave fellow was in a terribly exhausted conditian, but restor- atives being applied he recovered. The bravery of the ferrymen was highly applauded by the excited crowd, jpvito witnessed their gallant efforts to save the drowning 'man. The body of the excursionist has not yet been ,recovered.

div.head: A. RUSSIAN COUNT'S FIfIGT WITH A
div.p: A. RUSSIAN COUNT'S FIfIGT WITH A

BEAR. The Russian Public Administrator is advertising for the heirs of Count Skiermond, of the city of Kostoff-on- Don, who died from injuries inflicted by his pet bear the other day, leaving a fortune of two million roilbles. There are sundry relatives, hut their whereabouts is un- known. The count lived for years a secluded exis- tence in his castle, his only companions being a huge bear and a woman as housekeeper.. The bear, which, was very tame, roamed around the house, was on the best of terms with the master, and usually shared the nightly supply of strong liquors; in fact, Skiermond and the bear got drunk together. A short time ago the mas- ter and the bear quarrelled in their cups, and the man began to kick the hear. Bruin objected, and a sparring match 'ensued, which soon changed iito a catch-as- catch-can contest, both combatants doing their best to throttle mots other. Skeirinond, who had the strength of Hercules, was equal to the bear in every sense, and eventually was victorious, as he succeeded in strangling the hear. However, Co severely was he bitten and mauled in the combat, that he had to be dragged to bed by the housekeeper, where he remained several days, dying slowly from loss of blood and internal injuries.

Bowis.—The Ilaydock Bowling Club played their opening match on Saturday, against Billinge, on the Billinge ground. The game resulted in favour of the home players. WHITSUNTIDE. —The colliers employed by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., ceased work for the Whitsuntide holidays on Saturday, and sere allowed Whit Monday off. Work was, however, not general on Tuestlay, most of the men remaining out until Wednesday,

„ HAYDOCK CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The scholars attending this school had their annual field-day on Saturday afternoon. They assembled at the schools at Blackbrook, and headed by the Ashton Temperance Brass Band,. proceeded to Blackbrook Bridge, then through the village, and afterwards through the grounds of "The Heyes,” which had been thrown open to them by Mrs. Evans. After their tour of the grounds they repaired to the Hay-dock Schools, where tea awaited them. Afterwards they proceeded to a field near the residence of Mrs. Evans, which had been placed at their disposal, and the scholars seemed to appreciate the pleasures of the afternoon very much. The scholars were in charge of Messrs. Maddi4n, George Harrison, Rinuner, and John Latham, assisted by the teachers.

div.p: THE PARKSIDE WELL,

The No. 1 well is 80 feet in depth, and was carried out by Messrs. Timmins and Sons, of Run- corn, in 1879. A:boring is carried to a depth of 296 feet from the surface, the diameter is 14 to 10 inches, and the upper coal measures were proved at 291 feet.— The following details of the section, like those of the Winwick Boring, were noted after inspection of the samples obtained by the Messrs. The surface level of the Parkside and Winwick borings being the same, and the depth to the coal measures being respectively 181 and 231 feet below Ordnance Datum, their slope to the south is 50 feet in a mile. GOLBORNE PUMPING STATION. . .

Further north at Golborne is the Pumping Station of the Ince Waterworks. The surface level is 125 feet above Ordnance Datum, the well is 150 feet deep and 9 feet in diameter, at the bottom of which is a bore-hole 3 inches in diameter, to a total depth from the surface of 300 feet. The yield is 240,000 gallons per day, reducing the level of the water from 80 to 120 feet, which is restored after 6 hours rest. The works were established in 1871. The section is as follows :

Feet. 19 150 Pebble Beds 131 300 Details not given 150 The bottom of this boring is 175 feet below the Ordnance Datum line; whether it reached the coal measures, as is prebable, does not appear. Between Golborne and Parkside the Pebble Beds occur dipping east ; from Parkside to Spa Well they continue but gradually change their direction of dip to south-east, as is well seen in Middleton Hall Quarry. Had not this change.of "strike" taken place the base of the Pebble Beds would have cropped out north of Winwick, instead of which they occupy a considerable tract around Go!- borne, and the thickness of triassic strata would have been much less than at Winwick, 11 to the south, the strike of the works nearly coinciding in direction with a line drawn between the two wells. Below the Winwick pumping station and Dallam Lane Forge boring this is not the case; the Pebble Beds at Huhn° Delf, south of I Winwick, dip south, or directly towards Dallam, the amount varies from 4in. to Bin, in different quarries. taking it an average of 4in., and the base of the Red Sandstone at Winwick to be 231 feet below 0.1)., and assuming the surface of the coal measures beneath the Red Sandstone to correspond to the amount of dip, the base of the trias would be carried down 1,000 feet, or 1,231 feet below 0.D., or 1,277 below the surface, which is 46 feet above O.D. at the Dallam Lane Forge boring, which actually penetrated 880 feet of this amoul. COAL MEASURES UNDERLIE WARRINGTON.

There is therefore strong evidence that coal measures underlie Wa,rrington at a depth of about 400 yards. but at what angle, and in what direction there is at preseikt no proof. The highest coals of the Wigan Coalfields, the " Ince Mines "are striking nearly south, between Town Green, Ashton, Edge Green, and Golborne, and did no fault intervene their southern prolongation would pass through Newton Bridge, and Great Sankey, beneath the Red Sandstone,but they are repeatedlythrown westward by faults, with westerly downthrows, so that the coal measurest ;between Winwick and Sutton are entirely measures lying above the Lyon's Delf, of St. Helens, and probably in great part they belong to the Upper or Man- chester Coalfield, In the centre of this tract occurs the Bold Hall Colliery, east of St. Helens Junction, which I carefully examined some years ago, and believe the coal seams there found are not the equivalent of the St. Helens Coals, but belong to those of the Upper coal measures. Progressing westwards, the first fault with an easterly downthrow isthat passing through WhistoA, which, with that passing through Sutton Heath, throws in the remarkable triangle of New Red Sandstone, ex- tending from Rainhill to Eccleston Hill, and it will be noted that in this triangle is the small tract of Upper coal measure with Spirorhis Limestone. brought up by faults long since described by Professor Hull and Mr. Binney. Here we have the normal south-west, and north-east of this area, and should this continue eastwards, and the limestones proved at Winwick range in this direction with a south-easterly dip, the measures underlying the Red Sandstones at Warrington must be very much above the horizon of theSpirorbisLimestone,and be on a higher horizon of the Upper Coal measures than any previously occuring in Lancashire. But should the limestone at Win wick,like that of Iluyton .belong to the spirorbis lime- stone series of the Manchester coal-field, the Open- shaw coal may lie beneath the red-sandstone.at an attain- able depth at Warrington. That it is also possible that the depth will be found to be still greater, as it is not certain that the limestone may not belong to a horizon, at present not proved elsewhere, of later date, than any of the beds occurring at Manchester.
THE WORKING OF COAL WOULD NOT AFFECT WATER STIFFLY. •

I am of opinion that should these coals be worked at a depth of 200 or 400 yards from the surface, no evil effects can possibly arise as regards the quantity or quality of the water obtained. lam acquainted with the Hednesford pumping station of the South Stafford- shire Waterworks, in which the red sandstone is under- laid by coal measures, which are worked in adjicent collieries, without any deterioration of the water. This is also the case in some of the wells of the Staffordshire Potteries' Waterworks, and is the case at Collins Green Colliery, which is a pumping station for the St. Helens Corporation Water Supply, and at the Golborne pump- ing station of the Ince Waterworks, in your own area. It would be the aim and object of any colliery under- taking to sink a water-tight shaft, and to exclude the waters of the red sandstone, from running down into the e,.al workings. This is done most effectually by the shafts sunk by the Kind-Chaudron process in the Bel- gium coal-field, which pass through chalk full of water, from which the Belgium and North-East of francetowns are supplied with water, while the coal is wrought be- neath. The Manchester, or upper coal measures, and the Wigan, or the middle coal measures, are both largely made up of shales, and these are absolutely impervions to water, and support the rainfall, which is absorbed by the red sandstones above, just as those of Belgium sup- port the waters of the chalk. The water of the upper strata cannot possibly pass into the coal measures, or into the "workings" below, with properly constructed shafts, as are now universally carried out.

div.head: PROBABLE YIELD OF WATER.,
div.p: THE PROBABLE YIELD OF WATER.,

As regards the yield to be obtained from the red sand- ptone, in the area over which the Company has statutory powers, I am of opinion that it is capable of absorbing ten inches of the annual rainfall, or a quantity which will give a daily average of 400,000 gallons per square mile, over a very considerable portion of the Company's in,ako. The area at present drawn upon by the present works produces a very partial "cone of exhaustion" over about two square miles and a quarter, and is evidently Capable of some extension. By a new pumping station,

div.head: FIRE IN CATHERINE-ST.
div.p: THE FIRE IN CATHERINE-ST.

It was at first thought that the fire that took place at some stables in Catherine-st., early on Saturday morning last, had been caused by some- one sleeping on the premises having lighted a match, but it is now supposed that sparks from a passing train had dropped on the tarred roof of the build- ing, and set it on fire. div.head: ANNIVERSARY SERVICES AT MOORE.
div.p: ANNIVERSARY SERVICES AT MOORE.

The -anniversary services in connection with Moore Wesleyan sunday School were held on Sun- day, when special sermons were preached by Mr. John Bennett, of Bewsey, Warrington. There was a large congregation at each service, and the collec- tions realized £l4 17s. Bd. Special hymns were rendered by the children and choir. Miss Bessie Dutton was at the harmonium.

LOCAL DELEGATES TO THE ODDFELLOWS This year the Warripgton district is represented at the A.M.O. of the order, held at Ipswich, by P. Prov. G.M. John Emson, corresponding secretaiy of the Warrington district, and the secretary of the Loyal Admiral Nelson Lodge. Mr. Emson was first a delegate at Nottingham in the year 1883, and in the following year he was again chosen to repre- sent the Warrington Oddfellows at Nottingham. In the year 1886, he attended in the same capacity at Stafford, and two years ago he was delegate to the meeting at Gloucester. Mr. I. Rostron, head master of St. Luke's Schools, Blackburn, has been unanimously appointed by the executive as the day school lecturer and secretary of the juvenile section of the society and will com- mence on the let of September, when his services will be available for simple scientific temperance lectures in Church of England day schools, and for Band of Hope meetings in Warrington and neigh- bourhood and throughout the diocese of Liverpool. There were 38 candidates for the post.

div.head: FIRE AT MOORE
div.p: FIRE AT MOORE

There was an outbreak of fire at Moore on Satur- day afternoon At about 3.30 o'clock a spark from a chimney set fire to two thatched cottages at Moss Side, Moore, in the occupation of George Fleetwood and Joseph Woodcock, farm labourers in the service of Thomas Percival. Henry Woodcock, one of Joseph Woodcock's sons was at work in an adjoin- ing field when he saw the spark fall on the thatched roof, which was soon on fire, and in about an hour both the cottages were destroyed, the damage being estimated at about ..£l2O, which includes damage to furniture. The loss on the cottages, which belonged to sir Richard awoke, is not covered by insurance. So intense was the heat of the fire that a sum of .£3O in gold and silver, which had been kept in a box upstairs, is said to have been melted.

CRrraltutr. Huth eltraf4 Tailor. Bold-st. Warrimenn.—Arivt. MAY PROCESSIONS AT THE CATHOLIC CHURCHES On 'Sunday evening the annual May procession took place in St. Mary's (R.C.) Church, the Guild of the Children of Mary and the Confraternity of Mount Carmel being represented. Father Sumner (rector) walked at the end of the procession. Several handsome banners were carried b the young women of the guilds. During the offertory Mr. Richard Eccles sang the anthem for Whit-Sunday "Veni Sancto Spiritus." The altars were covered with flowers and illuminated with lighted candles. The May processions round the interior of St. Alban's took place at the evening service on Sunday, many young girls wearing beautifully worked banners. and others with veils upon theirheads walkinground the church. The building is about to be re-seated with pitchpine seats in place of the old pews, which have been in use sixty years. Messrs. Williams and Clay are proceeding with the Lady altar, which will be of different coloured marble. it is expected to be completed in a short time. Father Almond 0.5.8., late of St. Mary's, Buttermarket-street, is acting as the architect of the altar, which is of classic design

• THE SANIIEY-ST. Ctricus. Sampson. the strong man, has been one of the attractions at the Circus during the week, and his muscular display, and really startling feats of strength, have been witnessed by crowded audi- ences night after night. His pupil, Cyclops, is also a tower of strength. Sampson, among other things, can break in two with hi S fingers a shilling piece, as well as a chain bracelet on his right arm by the expansion of his muscles at a pressure, it is said, of 6,0001b5. Fastening a leather strap round his chest he soon succed in snapping it by an expansion of the lungs. Chains hung -between two poles were broken by a powerful blow from his fist. He and Cyclops performed other feats with the mammoth and other dumbells, singly and together, and Samp- son's last performance was a tug of war against 14 men out of the audience, the victory resting with " the Iron King." Altogether the performance was a remarkable one. and was quite equal to the expec- tations of the audience. The other features of the programme were, as usual, varied and novel, and taken as a whole Ohmy's Whit-week has from a Circus point of view been a great success. On Wednesday evening the Volunteer hand was in attendance. Hurst, the champion bicyclist, will fulfil an engagement at the Circus next week.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE CLUB FOR CULCHRTH.
div.p: A CONSERVATIVE CLUB FOR CULCHRTH.

OnSaturday liternoon, Mr. W. C. Jones. J.P.,. Conservative candidate for the Leigh Division, opened a new Conservative club at Culcheth, Amongst those present were Captain IWithington_ Mr. W. Marsh, Mr. J. Hartley. Mr. Walter Tune nicliffe, J.P.. Mr. A. Withingt on. Mr. R. Sephton, th Rev. Dr. Black, and Dr. R. F. Brideoalr. Mr. Jones congratulated the Conservatives of Culcheth upon 1) ri vi tig obtained such a commodious club, which he hoped would extend Conservative influence in the district. He also congratulated the President, Cap- tain Withington, on fixing the 71st birthday ot the Queen for so auspicious a ceremony, and wished that the new club might meet with every success. Csntain Withington remarked that they bad opened the club with 72 members, and he hoped to see that number largely increased. Mr. J. Hartley next addressed the meeting, and pointed out that the success of a club like that depended very much upon the management. The building was a handsome one, and he asked the members to strive not so much to convert the Liberals, but to get hold of that class who up to the present had not declared them- selves as leaning to any political party, and who voted first one way and then another. Mr. W. E. Marsh also spoke, and votes of thanks to Mr. Jones concluded the meeting. CRITCHIEVB Tailoring meets the Advt.

IN THE MATTER OF THE COMPANIES' ACT 1867, AND IN THE MATTER OF THE COMPANIES' ACT 1877, AND IN THE MATTER OF THE SAINT HELENS COPPER COMPANY, LIMITED. AND REDUCED. OTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that an office 11 copy of the Order of the High Court of Justice Chancery Division dated the 17th day of May. 1890, confirm- ing the cancellation and reduction of the capital of the above named Company from £lOO,OOO divided into 1.000 shares of £lOO each to £50,000 divided into 1,000 shares of £5O each. (1.) By reducing the liability on each share and the nominal amount of such share to the extent of £2O. (2.) By returning paid up carital to the extent of £3O on each share and reducing the nominal amount of such share to the same extent and the minute (approved by the Court) with respect to the capital of the Company, as altered in conformity with the provisions of the above Statutes were delivered to, and the original order registered by.the Registrar of Joint Stock Com- panies on the 23rd day of May, 1890. And further take notice that the said minute is in the words and figures following : " The Capital of the Saint Helens Copper Company, Limited, and Reduced, is from henceforth £50,000 divided into 1,000 shares of £5O each, which have been and are to be deemed fully paid up, instead of £lOO,OOO divided into 1,000 shares of £lOO each with £BO per share paid up." Dated this 23rd day of May, 1890. MARESOO PEAT CE, Abchurch Chambers, Abchurch Yard, London. Solicitor for the said Company.
